title: حِكَايَةُ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الثَّانِي
titleEn: The Tale of the Second Qalandar, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 86–98 (continuing directly from nights-12, whose text breaks off mid-sentence as the captive princess forces open the inscribed dome), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 13 opens still inside the underground vault: the efrit Jirjīs returns to find evidence the princess has had a visitor, tortures and finally kills her by his own jinn-law against an unfaithful wife, then confronts the Second Qalandar himself. Rather than kill him outright, the efrit offers him one plea, and the qalandar tells the embedded tale of al-Maḥsūd wa-l-Ḥāsid (the Envied Man and the Envier): a man harried by his jealous neighbor into exile and near-murder by a pushed fall down a well is saved by jinn, overhears from them the cure for a king’s possessed daughter, cures her, rises from son-in-law to vizier to king in turn — and, meeting his old persecutor again years later, forgives him outright rather than taking revenge. The efrit is unmoved: he lifts the qalandar into the air and transforms him into an ape. As an ape he wanders to the sea, boards a merchant ship under the captain’s protection, and wins a king’s favor by writing a beautiful hand — in turn, a five-couplet florilegium in five calligraphic styles (Ruqʿa, Rayhānī, Thuluth, Naskh, Ṭūmār) — and later a poem on roast meat, one on wine, and a chess victory over the king in two straight games, each marked with its own verse. The king’s daughter, the princess Sitt al-Ḥusn (“Lady of Beauty”), recognizes him at sight as an enchanted prince, not a beast, and reveals she herself learned sorcery as a girl; asked by her father to disenchant him, she agrees, and dawn cuts Shahrazad off as she takes up a knife to draw the first circle of her working against Jirjīs. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about violence (the mutilation and killing of the princess, the efrit’s transformation-curse) and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةَ عَشَرَ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْفَرَنْجِيَّ الثَّانِيَ قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ يَا سَيِّدَتِي لَهَا رَقَصَتِ الْقُبَّةُ رَقْصًا قَوِيًّا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithata ʿashara qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-faranjiyya al-thāniya qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati yā sayyidatī lahā raqaṣati al-qubbatu raqṣan qawiyyan
sentences.l: And when it was the thirteenth night, she said: 'It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the second Frank said to the girl, "O my lady" — for her the dome danced a mighty dance,
sentences.i: Now when it was the thirteenth night, she said: 'It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the second Frank said to the girl, "My lady!" — and on her account the very dome broke into a wild, violent dance,
sentences.n: The archive prints الْفَرَنْجِيَّ الثَّانِيَ, 'the second Frank,' exactly where the returning captor-efrit (named Jirjīs earlier in the tale) is expected; the wording is kept as printed and flagged rather than silently corrected, and الْعِفْرِيتُ a few sentences below is read as the same figure. لَهَا, 'for her' (third person), sits inside what otherwise reads as direct address to her (يَا سَيِّدَتِي); the shift of person is kept as printed, of a piece with this text's loose handling of pronoun person elsewhere in reported speech. الثَّالِثَةَ عَشَرَ again prints its ordinal without the expected عَشْرَةَ, as at the parallel spot in nights-12.

sentences.t: إِلَّا وَالْأَقْطَارُ قَدْ أَظْلَمَتْ وَأَرْعَدَتْ وَأَبْرَقَتْ وَهَزْهَزَتِ الْأَرْضَ وَأَطْبَقَتِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: illā wa-al-aqṭāru qad aẓlamat wa-arʿadat wa-abraqat wa-hazhazati al-arḍa wa-aṭbaqati al-dunyā
sentences.l: when, behold, the horizons had darkened, and thundered, and lightninged, and the earth had quaked, and the world had closed up —
sentences.i: when suddenly every quarter of the sky went black, and thundered, and flashed with lightning, and the earth shook, and the whole world seemed to shut in around us —
sentences.n: إِلَّا وَ… works here like the frame story's وَإِذَا, marking a sudden narrative turn ('and behold, suddenly'), not the ordinary restrictive 'only, except.' أَطْبَقَتِ الدُّنْيَا, 'the world closed up,' is the same idiom for blotting darkness used later in this same tale (اِنْطَبَقَتِ الدُّنْيَا) and in the frame story.

sentences.t: فَطَارَ الْكَسْرُ مِنْ رَاسِي وَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَا الْخَبَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭāra al-kasru min rāsī wa-qultu lahā mā al-khabaru
sentences.l: so the fracture flew from my head, and I said to her: 'What is the news?'
sentences.i: so my wits flew clean out of my head with fright, and I said to her: 'What has happened?'
sentences.n: طَارَ الْكَسْرُ مِنْ رَاسِي, literally 'the fracture flew from my head,' is obscure; it is rendered here by sense as a variant of the commoner idiom طَارَ عَقْلِي, 'my mind flew [with terror],' though الْكَسْر does not otherwise carry that meaning, and the phrase may be colloquial or corrupt in a way this note cannot resolve. رَاسِي is this text's colloquial spelling of Classical رَأْسِي, 'my head' — the same dropped hamza met later in the qalandar's own tale (رَاسَ الْجَبَلِ).

sentences.t: قَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ قَدْ وَصَلَ إِلَيْنَا مَا حَذَّرْتُكَ مِنْ هَذَا وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ أَذَيْتَنِي انْجُ بِنَفْسِكَ وَاطْلُعْ مِنَ الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي جِئْتَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: qāla al-ʿifrītu qad waṣala ilaynā mā ḥadhdhartuka min hādhā wa-Allāhi la-qad adhaytanī unju bi-nafsika wa-uṭluʿ mina al-makāni alladhī jiʾta minhu
sentences.l: The efrit said: 'What I warned you of has come upon us on account of this — by God, you have indeed harmed me! Save yourself, and go up from the place that you came from.'
sentences.i: The efrit said: 'Just what I warned you against has now befallen us because of this — by God, you have truly endangered me! Save yourself and climb back up the way you came.'
sentences.n: The efrit's warning is addressed to the narrator, not to the girl — a separate speech from the taunt in the sentence above, and the first point in the slice where الْعِفْرِيتُ is named outright rather than by the odd الفرنجي of the opening line.

sentences.t: فَمِنْ شِدَّةِ خَوْفِي نَسِيتُ مَرْكُوبِي وَفَاسِي
sentences.tr: fa-min shiddati khawfī nasītu markūbī wa-fāsī
sentences.l: So out of the intensity of my fear, I forgot my mount and my axe.
sentences.i: So great was my fear that I forgot my mount and my axe.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا طَلَعْتُ دَرَجَتَيْنِ وَالْتَفَتُّ لِأَنْظُرَ وَإِذَا بِالْأَرْضِ قَدِ انْشَقَّتْ وَطَلَعَ مِنْهَا عِفْرِيتٌ ذُو مَنْظَرٍ بَشِعٍ وَقَالَ مَا هَذِهِ الزَّعْجَةُ الَّتِي أَزْعَجَتْنِي بِهَا مَا مُصِيبَتُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṭalaʿtu darajatayni wa-iltafattu li-anẓura wa-idhā bi-al-arḍi qadi inshaqqat wa-ṭalaʿa minhā ʿifrītun dhū manẓarin bashiʿin wa-qāla mā hādhihi al-zaʿjatu allatī azʿajatnī bihā mā muṣībatuki
sentences.l: So when I had climbed two steps and turned to look, behold, the earth had split, and there rose up out of it an efrit of hideous appearance, and he said: 'What is this commotion that has alarmed me by it — what is your calamity?'
sentences.i: So when I had climbed two steps and turned to look back, behold, the earth had split open, and out of it rose an efrit of hideous appearance, who said: 'What is this uproar that has so alarmed me — what has befallen you?'
sentences.n: A new عِفْرِيتٌ appears here, indefinite and 'of hideous appearance'; the Arabic does not say outright whether this is the same figure as الْعِفْرِيتُ two sentences above (read there as Jirjīs, despite the printed الْفَرَنْجِيّ) or a second, different demon — the tale leaves it unresolved, and so does this note. بِهَا, 'by it, with it,' is the resumptive pronoun the relative clause needs because أَزْعَجَتْنِي بِـ, 'alarmed me with/by,' takes its cause with بِـ; 'this commotion that alarmed me' would otherwise leave that preposition stranded.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ مَا أَصَابَنِي شَيْءٌ غَيْرَ أَنَّ صَدْرِي ضَاقَ فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَشْرَبَ شَرَابًا يَشْرَحُ صَدْرِي فَاسْتَعْمَلْتُ قَلِيلًا وَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَقْضِيَ شُغْلًا فَتَثَاقَلَتْ عَلَيَّ رَاسِي فَوَقَعْتُ عَلَى الْقُبَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat mā aṣābanī shayʾun ghayra anna ṣadrī ḍāqa fa-aradtu an ashraba sharāban yashraḥu ṣadrī fa-istaʿmaltu qalīlan wa-aradtu an aqḍiya shughlan fa-tathāqalat ʿalayya rāsī fa-waqaʿtu ʿalā al-qubbati
sentences.l: So she said: 'Nothing has befallen me, except that my chest grew tight, so I wanted to drink a drink that would open my chest, so I used a little; and I wanted to attend to a task, and my head grew heavy upon me, and I fell upon the dome.'
sentences.i: So she said: 'Nothing is wrong with me — only that my chest felt tight, so I meant to drink something to ease it, and I took a little; then I meant to go and see to something, and my head grew heavy on me, and I fell upon the dome.'
sentences.n: عَلَيَّ رَاسِي, 'my head [grew heavy] upon me,' repeats the colloquial spelling رَاسِي already met above, kept as printed rather than restored to رَأْسِي.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ تَكْذِبِي يَا قَحْبَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ʿifrītu takdhibī yā qaḥbatu
sentences.l: So the efrit said to her: 'You lie, O whore!'
sentences.i: But the efrit said to her: 'You are lying, you whore!'
sentences.n: تَكْذِبِي prints the plain indicative rather than a jussive/imperative form; read here as a flat accusation, 'you are lying' (not 'do not lie').

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَ فِي الْقَصْرِ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَرَأَى الْمَرْكُوبَ وَالنَّاسَ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓara fī al-qaṣri yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-raʾā al-markūba wa-al-nāsa
sentences.l: And he looked about the chamber, right and left, and he saw the mount and the men.
sentences.i: And he looked around the chamber, right and left, and caught sight of the mount and the men's traces.
sentences.n: الْمَرْكُوبَ وَالنَّاسَ, 'the mount and the men,' recalls مَرْكُوبِي, 'my mount,' left behind two sentences above — the very evidence of a visitor that gives the efrit his proof. فَرَأَى keeps the archive's own precomposed hamza-on-alif, one of the small set of words the edition prints that way rather than bare.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَا هَذَا إِلَّا لِبْسُ الْإِنْسِ مَنْ جَاءَ إِلَى عِنْدِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā hādhā illā libsu al-insi man jāʾa ilā ʿindiki
sentences.l: So he said to her: 'This is nothing but the trace of a human — someone who came to your place.'
sentences.i: So he said to her: 'This is nothing but a human's mark — someone has been coming to you.'
sentences.n: لِبْس is used here in the sense of a trace or mark left behind, 'the touch of a human,' rather than 'clothing' in the ordinary sense — the mount and men just seen are read by the efrit as proof that a human being has been visiting her.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ مَا نَظَرْتُ هَذَا إِلَّا السَّاعَةَ كَأَنَّهُمَا تَعَلَّقَا مَعَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat mā naẓartu hādhā illā al-sāʿata kaʾannahumā taʿallaqā maʿaka
sentences.l: So she said: 'I did not see this except just now — as if the two of them had attached themselves with you.'
sentences.i: So she said: 'I only just noticed it this very moment — it is as if the two of them had come along attached to you.'
sentences.n: كَأَنَّهُمَا, 'as if the two of them,' is left without a stated antecedent; most likely the mount and the men just named, which she suggests, by way of excuse, must somehow have come along with the efrit himself rather than with any visitor of hers.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ هَذَا كَلَامٌ مُحَالٌ مَا يَنْطَلِي عَلَيَّ يَا كُورَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu hādhā kalāmun muḥālun mā yanṭalī ʿalayya yā kūratu
sentences.l: So the efrit said: 'This is impossible talk — it does not go down smoothly on me, O ball!'
sentences.i: So the efrit said: 'This is nonsense — it won't wash with me, you slut!'
sentences.n: يَنْطَلِي عَلَى is the colloquial idiom, still current, for a lie or trick 'going down, being swallowed' by someone; negated here, 'it will not work on me.' يَا كُورَة is an insult, literally 'ball' — likely short for كُورَةُ زِبْل, 'dung-ball,' a term of abuse for a woman comparable to English 'slut, trollop.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ عَرَّاهَا وَشَتَمَهَا بَيْنَ أَرْبَعَ سِكَكٍ وَجَعَلَ يُعَاقِبُهَا وَيُقَرِّرُهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu ʿarrāhā wa-shatamahā bayna arbaʿa sikakin wa-jaʿala yuʿāqibuhā wa-yuqarriruhā
sentences.l: Then indeed he stripped her, and he cursed her between four lanes, and he began to punish her and to interrogate her,
sentences.i: Then he stripped her naked, and cursed her before all four lanes to hear, and set about beating her and pressing her for the truth,
sentences.n: بَيْنَ أَرْبَعَ سِكَكٍ, literally 'between four lanes,' pictures the abuse happening in the open, at a crossroads, for all to see — rendered idiomatically as public humiliation. يُقَرِّرُ carries its judicial sense here, 'to press for a confession, interrogate,' not the ordinary 'to decide, establish.'

sentences.t: فَمَا كَانَ وَلَا هَانَ عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَسْمَعَ بُكَاهَا فَطَلَعْتُ مِنَ السُّلَّمِ وَأَنَا مِنَ الْخَوْفِ أَرْجُفُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā kāna wa-lā hāna ʿalayya an asmaʿa bukāhā fa-ṭalaʿtu mina al-sullami wa-anā mina al-khawfi arjufu
sentences.l: So it neither was nor was it easy for me to hear her weeping; so I climbed up from the stairway, and I, out of fear, was trembling.
sentences.i: I could not bear, could not stand, to go on listening to her weeping, so I climbed up the stairs, trembling with fear.
sentences.n: مَا كَانَ وَلَا هَانَ عَلَيَّ is a doubled negation for emphasis, roughly 'it neither was [bearable] nor was it easy for me' — rendered as a single intensified 'I could not bear.'

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى أَعْلَا الْمَوْضِعِ وَرَدَّيْتُ الطَّابَقَ كَمَا كَانَ وَسَتَرْتُهُ بِالتُّرَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣaltu ilā aʿlā al-mawḍiʿi wa-raddaytu al-ṭābaqa kamā kāna wa-satartuhu bi-al-turābi
sentences.l: So when I arrived at the top of the place, I put back the slab as it had been, and I covered it with the earth.
sentences.i: So when I reached the top, I put the trapdoor back just as it had been, and covered it over with earth.
sentences.n: رَدَّيْتُ is this text's spelling of Classical رَدَدْتُ, 'I put back' — the same yāʾ-for-doubled-consonant spelling met in nights-12's رَدَّيْنَا. الطَّابَق, 'slab, trapdoor,' names the same covering as in that earlier passage.

sentences.t: وَنَدِمْتُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلْتُ غَايَةَ النَّدَمِ
sentences.tr: wa-nadimtu ʿalā mā faʿaltu ghāyata al-nadami
sentences.l: And I regretted what I had done, the utmost of regret.
sentences.i: And I regretted what I had done, more bitterly than I can say.
sentences.n: غَايَةَ النَّدَمِ is the same cognate-accusative intensifier met repeatedly in nights-12 (cf. زَجْرًا بَلِيغًا, غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ).

sentences.t: وَتَذَكَّرْتُ الصَّبِيَّةَ وَحُسْنَهَا وَكَيْفَ يُعَاقِبُهَا هَذَا الْمَلْعُونُ وَكَيْفَ لَهَا خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ سَنَةً وَمَا جَرَى لَهَا بِسَبَبِي
sentences.tr: wa-tadhakkartu al-ṣabiyyata wa-ḥusnahā wa-kayfa yuʿāqibuhā hādhā al-malʿūnu wa-kayfa lahā khamsatun wa-ʿishrūna sanatan wa-mā jarā lahā bi-sababī
sentences.l: And I remembered the girl, and her beauty, and how this accursed one was punishing her, and how she has had twenty-five years, and what had befallen her because of me.
sentences.i: And I thought of the girl, and her beauty, and how this accursed creature was beating her, and how she had already spent twenty-five years down here, and all that had now befallen her because of me.
sentences.n: كَيْفَ لَهَا خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ سَنَةً, literally 'how there are to her twenty-five years,' idiomatically 'how she has [already spent] twenty-five years' — the same span of her captivity given in the frame summary of this tale.

sentences.t: وَافْتَكَرْتُ أَبِي وَمَمْلَكَةً وَكَيْفَ صِرْتُ حَطَّابًا
sentences.tr: wa-iftakartu abī wa-mamlakatan wa-kayfa ṣirtu ḥaṭṭāban
sentences.l: And I recalled my father, and a kingdom, and how I had become a woodcutter.
sentences.i: And I thought back on my father, and on a kingdom, and on how I had come to be a woodcutter.
sentences.n: مَمْلَكَةً is printed indefinite and without any possessive, where sense expects 'my kingdom' (مَمْلَكَتِي); kept as printed rather than silently supplied. اِفْتَكَرْتُ, 'I recalled,' is colloquial (form VIII of فكر), beside the more Classical تَفَكَّرْتُ used earlier in nights-12.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ أَنْ صَفَا الْوَقْتُ رَجَعَ تَكَدَّرَ عَيْشِي فَبَكَيْتُ وَقُلْتُ هَذَا الْبَيْتُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda an ṣafā al-waqtu rajaʿa takaddara ʿayshī fa-bakaytu wa-qultu hādhā al-baytu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And after the time had grown calm, my life turned, grew turbid, once again; so I wept, and I recited this verse:
sentences.i: And just when things had settled, my life turned bitter once more; so I wept, and spoke this verse:
sentences.n: رَجَعَ تَكَدَّرَ عَيْشِي strings two verbs for one subject with no conjunction between them, literally 'my life turned, grew turbid' — read here as the idiomatic doubling رَجَعَ + verb for 'did X again,' i.e. 'my life grew turbid once more.'

sentences.t: إِذَا مَا أَنَاكَ الدَّهْرُ يَوْمًا بِنَكْبَةٍ * فَيَوْمًا تَرَى يُسْرًا وَيَوْمًا تَرَى عُسْرًا
sentences.tr: idhā mā anāka al-dahru yawman bi-nakbatin * fa-yawman tarā yusran wa-yawman tarā ʿusran
sentences.l: If Fate should ever bring you, one day, a calamity, * then one day you will see ease, and one day you will see hardship.
sentences.i: If Time should ever visit a misfortune on you one day, * then one day you shall see ease, and one day hardship.
sentences.n: أَنَاكَ, 'brought you,' is a rare variant of أَتَاكَ, 'came to you' (i.e. 'brought upon you'); copied character for character from the archive, as verse requires, with no repointing.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَشَيْتُ إِلَى أَنِ أَتَيْتُ رَفِيقِي الْخَيَّاطَ فَلَقِيتُهُ مِنْ أَجْلِي عَلَى مَقَالِي النَّارِ وَهُوَ لِي فِي الِانْتِظَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma mashaytu ilā ani ataytu rafīqī al-khayyāṭa fa-laqītuhu min ajlī ʿalā maqālī al-nāri wa-huwa lī fī al-intiẓār
sentences.l: Then I walked on until I came to my friend the tailor, and I found him — on my account — upon the fire's griddles, and he was in waiting for me,
sentences.i: Then I walked on until I reached my friend the tailor, and found him worried sick on my account, as if upon live coals, waiting for me,
sentences.n: مَقَالِي النَّارِ, literally 'the griddles of the fire,' is read as an intensified idiom for anguished waiting (cf. the common expression 'his heart is on the fire'); مَقَالِي is the broken plural of مِقْلَى, 'frying-pan, griddle.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ إِنِّي بِتُّ الْبَارِحَةَ قَلْبِي عِنْدَكَ وَ خِفْتُ عَلَيْكَ مِنْ وَحْشٍ وَغَيْرِهِ فَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى سَلَامَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla innī bittu al-bāriḥata qalbī ʿindaka wa-khiftu ʿalayka min waḥshin wa-ghayrihi fa-al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi ʿalā salāmatika
sentences.l: so he said: 'Indeed I spent last night, my heart with you, and I feared for you from a wild beast or other; so praise be to God for your safety.'
sentences.i: and he said: 'I spent all last night with my heart at your side, fearing some wild beast or worse had befallen you — but praise God for your safety.'
sentences.n: بِتُّ الْبَارِحَةَ قَلْبِي عِنْدَكَ, literally 'I spent last night, my heart with you,' is an idiom of anxious concern through the night; قَلْبِي عِنْدَكَ stands as its own nominal clause describing the state he was in.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرْتُهُ عَلَى شَفَقَتِهِ عَلَيَّ وَدَخَلْتُ خَلْوَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-shakartuhu ʿalā shafaqatihi ʿalayya wa-dakhaltu khalwatī
sentences.l: So I thanked him for his kindness to me, and I entered my (private) chamber,
sentences.i: So I thanked him for his kindness, and went into my chamber,
sentences.n: خَلْوَتِي, 'my private chamber,' names the same lodging whose floor conceals the trapdoor to the underground vault, as the next sentences make clear.

sentences.t: وَجَعَلْتُ أَتَفَكَّرُ فِيمَا جَرَى لِي وَلُمْتُ نَفْسِي عَلَى كَثْرَةِ فُضُولِي وَرَفْضِي هٰذِهِ الْقُبَّةَ
sentences.tr: wa-jaʿaltu atafakkaru fīmā jarā lī wa-lumtu nafsī ʿalā kathrati fuḍūlī wa-rafḍī hādhihi al-qubbata
sentences.l: and I fell to reflecting on what had happened to me, and I blamed myself for the excess of my curiosity and my casting-off of this dome,
sentences.i: and I fell to brooding over all that had happened to me, and blamed myself for my excessive curiosity and for having refused to leave this dome alone,
sentences.n: وَرَفْضِي هٰذِهِ الْقُبَّةَ, literally 'my rejecting/discarding of this dome,' is puzzling taken strictly ('rejection' of what?); it is read here as 'my refusal to leave it be' — i.e. he blames himself both for prying and for having gone on to force open the trapdoor despite knowing better. القُبَّة, 'the dome,' names the domed stone covering he lifted to find the staircase down to the vault, told earlier in this same tale.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا فِي هٰذَا الْحِسَابِ وَإِذَا بِصَدِيقِي الْخَيَّاطِ دَخَلَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-anā fī hādhā al-ḥisābi wa-idhā bi-ṣadīqī al-khayyāṭi dakhala ʿalayya
sentences.l: And I being in this reckoning, behold, with my friend the tailor — he came in to me,
sentences.i: And while I was turning this over in my mind, all at once my friend the tailor came in to me,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِي يَا فَتَى بَرَّا شَيْخٌ عَجَمِيٌّ يَطْلُبُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lī yā fatā barrā shaykhun ʿajamiyyun yaṭlubuka
sentences.l: and he said to me: 'O young man, outside [there is] a foreign old man asking for you,'
sentences.i: and said to me: 'O young man, there is an old foreign gentleman outside asking for you,'
sentences.n: بَرَّا is colloquial for Classical خَارِجًا/بَرَّةَ, 'outside' — kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَمَعَهُ فَاسُكَ وَمَرْكُوبُ رِجْلِكَ قَدْ جَاءَ بِهِمَا إِلَى الْخَيَّاطِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-maʿahu fāsuka wa-markūbu rijlika qad jāʾa bihimā ilā al-khayyāṭīna
sentences.l: and with him your axe and your foot's mount — he has come with the two of them to the tailors,'
sentences.i: and with him is your axe and the rope for your foot — he has brought the two of them to the tailors' quarter,'
sentences.n: مَرْكُوبُ رِجْلِكَ, literally 'the mount of your foot,' is read here as the rope-loop you set a foot in to descend into the pit — the same implement the text calls التَّرْجِيل a few lines on, apparently from رِجْل, 'foot, leg.'

sentences.t: وَقُلْ لَهُمْ لَهُمْ أَنَا خَرَجْتُ وَقْتَ أَذَانِ الْمُؤَذِّنِ إِلَى صَلَوةِ الْفَجْرِ فَعَثَرْتُ بِهِمَا وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ لِمَنْ هُمَا دُلُّونِي عَلَى صَاحِبِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-qul lahum lahum anā kharajtu waqta adhāni al-muʾadhdhini ilā ṣalawti al-fajri fa-ʿathartu bihimā wa-lam aʿlam liman humā dullūnī ʿalā ṣāḥibihimā
sentences.l: and say to them, to them: I went out at the time of the muezzin's call, to the dawn prayer, and I stumbled upon the two of them, and I did not know to whom the two of them belonged; direct me to their owner —'
sentences.i: and tell them: I went out at the muezzin's call to the dawn prayer, and I chanced upon these two, not knowing whose they were; so direct me to their owner —'
sentences.n: لَهُمْ لَهُمْ prints the same word twice running; almost certainly a compositor's dittography rather than a meaningful repetition, and kept as printed rather than silently reduced to one. صَلَوة keeps the edition's older spelling with wāw for the tāʾ marbūṭa of صَلَاة, as in the frame story's وَالصَّلَوةُ.

sentences.t: فَدَلُّوهُ الْخَيَّاطِينَ عَلَيْكَ وَقَدْ عَرَفُوا فَاسَكَ وَهُوَ قَاعِدٌ فِي دُكَّانِي
sentences.tr: fa-dallūhu al-khayyāṭīna ʿalayka wa-qad ʿarafū fāsaka wa-huwa qāʿidun fī dukkānī
sentences.l: so the tailors directed him to you — and they recognized your axe as it sat in my shop —
sentences.i: so the tailors sent him on to you, for they recognized your axe sitting there in my shop,
sentences.n: دَلُّوهُ … الْخَيَّاطِينَ carries a plural verb although its subject الْخَيَّاطِينَ follows it — the same non-Classical agreement met throughout this text (cf. وَقَالُوا لَهُ الْخُدَّامُ elsewhere in this tale).

sentences.t: فَاخْرُجْ إِلَيْهِ وَاشْكُرْهُ وَخُذْ فَاسَكَ وَتَرْجِيلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ukhruj ilayhi wa-ushkurhu wa-khudh fāsaka wa-tarjīlaka
sentences.l: so go out to him, and thank him, and take your axe and your rope.'

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ اِصْفَرَّ لَوْنِي وَتَغَيَّرَ كَوْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu hādhā al-kalāma iṣfarra lawnī wa-taghayyara kawnī
sentences.l: So when I heard this speech, my color paled, and my being changed —
sentences.i: So when I heard this, the color drained from my face, and my whole state changed within me —
sentences.n: لَوْنِي / كَوْنِي is a rhymed pair (sajʿ), 'my hue' and 'my very being,' pointing up the shock of the news.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِأَرْضِ خَلْوَتِي انْشَقَّتْ وَطَلَعَ مِنْهَا الْعَجَمِيُّ وَإِذَا هُوَ الْعِفْرِيتُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā kadhālika wa-idhā bi-arḍi khalwatī inshaqqat wa-ṭalaʿa minhā al-ʿajamiyyu wa-idhā huwa al-ʿifrītu
sentences.l: And while I was thus, behold, with the floor of my chamber — it split open, and the foreign old man came up out of it; and behold, he was the efrit —
sentences.i: And while I stood there like that, all at once the floor of my chamber split open, and the old foreigner rose up out of it — and behold, he was the efrit —

sentences.t: وَقَدْ كَانَ عَاقَبَ الصَّبِيَّةَ غَايَةَ الْعِقَابِ فَلَمْ تُقِرَّ لَهُ بِشَيْءٍ فَأَخَذَ الْفَاسَ وَالتَّرْجِيلَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad kāna ʿāqaba al-ṣabiyyata ghāyata al-ʿiqābi fa-lam tuqirra lahu bi-shayʾin fa-akhadha al-fāsa wa-al-tarjīla
sentences.l: and he had already punished the girl with the utmost punishment, and she had not confessed to him anything; so he took the axe and the rope,
sentences.i: he had already punished the girl most severely, and she had confessed nothing to him; so he took up the axe and the rope,
sentences.n: غَايَةَ الْعِقَابِ is the same cognate-accusative-style intensifier found throughout this narrative (cf. زَجْرًا بَلِيغًا elsewhere in this tale).

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا إِنْ كُنْتِ جِرْجِيسَ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ إِبْلِيسَ فَأَنَا أَجِيءُ بِصَاحِبِ هٰذَا الْفَاسِ وَالتَّرْجِيلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā in kunti Jirjīsa min dhurriyyati Iblīsa fa-anā ajīʾu bi-ṣāḥibi hādhā al-fāsi wa-al-tarjīli
sentences.l: and said to her: 'Even if you were Jirjīs, of the offspring of Iblīs, I would still bring the owner of this axe and this rope.'
sentences.i: and said to her: 'Even were you Jirjīs himself, of the very brood of Iblīs, I would still fetch the owner of this axe and rope.'
sentences.n: جِرْجِيس is a proper name of a jinn-chief in Islamic jinn-lore; the efrit's boast is that no disguise or defiance on her part, however demonic, could stop him from finding the man out.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَاءَ فِي هٰذِهِ الْحِيلَةِ إِلَى الْحُطَّابِينَ وَدَخَلَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: thumma jāʾa fī hādhihi al-ḥīlati ilā al-ḥuṭṭābīna wa-dakhala ʿalayya
sentences.l: Then he came, in this ruse, to the woodcutters, and came in to me —
sentences.i: So he came, in this disguise, among the woodcutters, and came in to me —
sentences.n: الْحُطَّابِينَ, 'the woodcutters,' parallels الْخَيَّاطِينَ, 'the tailors,' above — the efrit works the same ruse on whichever guild the narrator happens to belong to at that point in the story.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يُمْهِلْنِي بَلِ اخْتَطَفَنِي وَطَارَ وَعَلَا بِي وَنَزَلَ وَغَاصَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَأَنَا لَا أَعْلَمُ بِنَفْسِي
sentences.tr: wa-lam yumhilnī bal ikhtaṭafanī wa-ṭāra wa-ʿalā bī wa-nazala wa-ghāṣa fī al-arḍi wa-anā lā aʿlamu bi-nafsī
sentences.l: and he gave me no respite, but rather snatched me up, and flew, and rose with me, and descended, and plunged into the earth, while I knew nothing of myself,
sentences.i: and he gave me no respite at all, but seized me, flew up, then dropped and plunged into the earth, while I lost all awareness of myself,

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَلَعَ بِي الْقَصْرَ الَّذِي كُنْتُ فِيهِ فَرَأَيْتُ الصَّبِيَّةَ عُرْيَانَةً مَشْبُوحَةً وَالدَّمُ يَسِيلُ مِنْ أَجْنَابِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma ṭalaʿa bī al-qaṣra alladhī kuntu fīhi fa-raʾaytu al-ṣabiyyata ʿuryānatan mashbūḥatan wa-al-damu yasīlu min ajnābihā
sentences.l: then he came up with me into the palace in which I had been, and I saw the girl, naked, stretched-out, with the blood flowing from her sides,
sentences.i: then he brought me up straight into the same underground palace where I had once been, and I saw the girl — stripped bare and stretched out, blood running from her sides,
sentences.n: الْقَصْر, 'the palace,' is this tale's own name for the underground chamber, told of earlier; طَلَعَ بِي, literally 'came up with me,' means he surfaced from his dive through the earth directly inside it.

sentences.t: فَذَرَفَتْ عَيْنَايَ بِالدَّمْعِ
sentences.tr: fa-dharafat ʿaynāya bi-al-damʿi
sentences.l: so my two eyes shed tears.
sentences.i: and my eyes filled with tears.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا كُورَةُ أَمَا هٰذَا هُوَ عَشِيقُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahā al-ʿifrītu wa-qāla lahā yā kūratu amā hādhā huwa ʿashīquki
sentences.l: So the efrit took hold of her and said to her: 'O Kūra, now — is this your lover?'
sentences.i: So the efrit seized her and said to her: 'Now then, Kūra — is this your lover?'
sentences.n: يَا كُورَةُ is obscure: كُورَة elsewhere means 'ball' or 'district, region,' neither an obvious form of address, and no clearly better reading suggests itself; kept and pointed as printed rather than silently emended.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ لَا أَعْرِفُ هٰذَا وَلَا رَأَيْتُهُ إِلَّا فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilayya wa-qālat lahu lā aʿrifu hādhā wa-lā raʾaytuhu illā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: So she looked at me and said to him: 'I do not know this man, nor have I seen him except in this hour.'
sentences.i: So she looked at me and said to him: 'I do not know this man, and I have never seen him before this very hour.'
sentences.n: A lie told to protect him; the qalandar, narrating his own tale, lets the reader see it as one, though nothing in her wording marks it as such.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ وَهٰذِهِ الْعُقُوبَةُ وَلَمْ تُقِرِّي فَقَالَتْ مَا رَأَيْتُهُ عُمْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ʿifrītu wa-hādhihi al-ʿuqūbatu wa-lam tuqirrī fa-qālat mā raʾaytuhu ʿumrī
sentences.l: So the efrit said to her: 'And this is the punishment, and still you will not confess?' So she said: 'I have never seen him, my whole life.'
sentences.i: The efrit said to her: 'And after this punishment, still you won't confess?' But she said: 'I have never seen him in my life.'

sentences.t: وَمَا يَحِلُّ مِنَ اللَّهِ أَنْ أَكْذِبَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā yaḥillu mina Allāhi an akdhiba ʿalayhi
sentences.l: 'and it is not licit, from God, that I should lie about him.'
sentences.i: 'And, before God, it would not be right for me to lie about him.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ إِنْ كُنْتِي لَمْ تَعْرِفِيهِ خُذِي هٰذَا السَّيْفَ وَاضْرِبِي عُنُقَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ʿifrītu in kuntī lam taʿrifīhi khudhī hādhā al-sayfa wa-uḍribī ʿunuqahu
sentences.l: So the efrit said to her: 'If you truly do not know him, take this sword and strike his neck.'
sentences.i: So the efrit said to her: 'If you really don't know him, take this sword and strike off his head.'
sentences.n: كُنْتِي keeps a colloquial extra يَاء on the 2fs perfect كُنْتِ — kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتِ السَّيْفَ وَجَاءَتْنِي وَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى رَاسِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhati al-sayfa wa-jāʾatnī wa-waqafat ʿalā rāsī
sentences.l: So she took the sword, and came to me, and stood over my head.
sentences.n: رَاسِي is the colloquial spelling of Classical رَأْسِي, 'my head' — the hamza simply not pronounced, and not printed, as with رَاسَكَ and رُحْ elsewhere in this tale.

sentences.t: فَأَشَارَتْ لَهَا بِحَاجِبَيْهَا وَدَمْعِي يَجْرِي عَلَى وَجْنَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-ashārat lahā bi-ḥājibayhā wa-damʿī yajrī ʿalā wajnatī
sentences.l: Then she gestured — to her — with her eyebrows, while my tears ran down my cheeks,
sentences.i: Then she signaled to him with her eyebrows, while my tears ran down my cheeks,
sentences.n: The Arabic literally reads لَهَا, 'to her'; translated here as 'to him' (the narrator), since the whole passage is about a silent exchange directed at him, and لَهُ/لَهَا differ by a single alif — a plausible copying slip, kept and pointed exactly as printed.

sentences.t: فَفَهِمَتْ إِشَارَتِي وَغَمَزَتْنِي وَقَالَتْ فَعَلْتَ بِنَا كُلَّ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-fahimat ishāratī wa-ghamazatnī wa-qālat faʿalta binā kulla hādhā
sentences.l: and she understood my signal, and winked at me, and said: 'You have done all this to us.'
sentences.i: and she read what I was silently telling her, gave me a wink, and said: 'You have brought all this upon us.'

sentences.t: فَأَشَرْتُ لَهَا أَنَّ هٰذَا وَقْتُ الْعَفْوِ وَلِسَانُ حَالِي يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-asharttu lahā anna hādhā waqtu al-ʿafwi wa-lisānu ḥālī yaqūlu
sentences.l: so I signaled to her that this was the time for pardon; and the tongue of my condition spoke:
sentences.i: so I signaled back to her that now was the moment for clemency; and what my silence said was this:
sentences.n: لِسَانُ حَالِي يَقُولُ, literally 'the tongue of my state says,' is the standard formula introducing a verse as expressing an unspoken condition, here quite literally so, since neither of them dares speak aloud.

sentences.t: يُتَرْجِمُ طَرْفِي عَنْ لِسَانِي فَتَعْلَمُوا * وَيُبْدِي الْهَوَى مَا فِي ضَمِيرِي أَكْتُمُ
sentences.tr: yutarjimu ṭarfī ʿan lisānī fa-taʿlamū * wa-yubdī al-hawā mā fī ḍamīrī aktumu
sentences.l: My glance interprets on behalf of my tongue, that you may know; * and passion reveals what, in my inmost self, I conceal.
sentences.i: My glance speaks for my tongue, that you may understand; and passion betrays what I keep hidden, deep within.
sentences.n: Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be — the pointing is the edition's own. This bayt opens the qalandar's own four verses on lovers who can communicate only through glances, since speech would betray them.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا الْتَقَيْنَا وَالدُّمُوعُ سَوَاجِمٌ * خَرِسْتُ وَطَرْفِي عَنْكُمُ يَتَكَلَّمُ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā al-taqaynā wa-al-dumūʿu sawājimu * kharistu wa-ṭarfī ʿankumu yatakallamu
sentences.l: And when we met, with the tears pouring down, * I fell mute, while my glance spoke in your stead.
sentences.i: And when we met, tears streaming down, I fell silent — it was my glance that spoke for me, to you.

sentences.t: تُشِيرُ فَأَدْرِي مَا تَقُولُ بِطَرْفِهَا * وَأُومِي إِلَيْهَا بِالْبَنَانِ فَتَفْهَمُ
sentences.tr: tushīru fa-adrī mā taqūlu bi-ṭarfihā * wa-ūmī ilayhā bi-al-banāni fa-tafhamu
sentences.l: She gestures, and I perceive what she says with her glance; * and I signal to her with the fingertips, and she understands.
sentences.i: She gestures, and I know at once what her glance is telling me; I signal back to her with my fingertips, and she understands.
sentences.n: الْبَنَان, 'fingertips,' names the second silent channel alongside the glance and the eyebrow, completing the poem's small repertoire of wordless signs.

sentences.t: حَوَاجِبُنَا تَقْضِي الْحَوَائِجَ بَيْنَنَا * وَنَحْنُ سُكُوتٌ وَالْهَوَى يَتَكَلَّمُ
sentences.tr: ḥawājibunā taqḍī al-ḥawāʾija baynanā * wa-naḥnu sukūtun wa-al-hawā yatakallamu
sentences.l: Our eyebrows settle the needs between us; * and we are silent, while passion speaks.
sentences.i: Our eyebrows settle all that passes between us, while we ourselves stay silent, and passion does the speaking.
sentences.n: حَوَاجِبُنَا تَقْضِي الْحَوَائِجَ is a paronomastic play on the root ح-و-ج (ḥawājib, 'eyebrows,' against ḥawāʾij, 'needs, matters'), closing the poem on the theme announced in its first line — the eye standing in for the tongue.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا فَرَغْتُ مِنَ الشِّعْرِ يَا سَيِّدَتِي رَمَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ السَّيْفَ مِنْ يَدِهَا
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā faraghtu mina al-shiʿri yā sayyidatī ramati al-ṣabiyyatu al-sayfa min yadihā
sentences.l: He said: 'Now when I had finished the poem — O my lady — the young woman threw the sword from her hand,
sentences.i: He said: 'Now when I had finished my verses — O my lady — the young woman let the sword fall from her hand,
sentences.n: قَالَ resumes the second qalandar's own first-person account, just after verses he had recited before this slice begins; يَا سَيِّدَتِي, addressed to the presiding lady of the house mid-sentence, matches يَا سِتِّي in the model's frame material.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ كَيْفَ أَضْرِبُ عُنُقَ مَنْ لَا أَعْرِفُهُ وَلَا أَسَاءَ عَلَيَّ مَا يَحِلُّ هَذَا فِي دِينِي وَتَأَخَّرَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat kayfa aḍribu ʿunuqa man lā aʿrifuhu wa-lā asāʾa ʿalayya mā yaḥillu hādhā fī dīnī wa-taʾakhkharat
sentences.l: and she said: 'How should I strike the neck of one whom I do not know, and who has not wronged me? This is not lawful in my religion.' And she held back.
sentences.i: and she said: 'How could I strike off the neck of a man I do not even know, and who has never done me wrong? My faith does not permit this.' And she hesitated, holding back.
sentences.n: أَسَاءَ already carries its own final ء in the archive, kept precomposed (the edition prints it that way); its opening hamza, like أَضْرِبُ's and أَعْرِفُ's, is editorially supplied on a plain alif the edition prints bare.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ مَا يَهُونُ عَلَيْكِي قَتْلُ مَحْبُوبِكِ كَوْنُهُ نَامَ مَعَكِ لَيْلَةً تُقَاسِي هَذِهِ الْعُقُوبَةَ وَلَا تُقِرِّي عَلَيْهِ وَبَعْدَ هَذَا لَا يَحِنُّ عَلَى الْجِنْسِ إِلَّا الْجِنْسُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu mā yahūnu ʿalaykī qatlu maḥbūbiki kawnuhu nāma maʿaki laylatan tuqāsī hādhihi al-ʿuqūbata wa-lā tuqirrī ʿalayhi wa-baʿda hādhā lā yaḥinnu ʿalā al-jinsi illā al-jinsu
sentences.l: Then the efrit said: 'It is no light thing for you — the killing of your beloved — merely because he slept with you one night, that you should endure this punishment and not confess against him? And after all this, no kind is tender to a kind but its own kind.'
sentences.i: The efrit said: 'So sparing your beloved's life is too hard for you to give up — though he only lay with you once — that you would rather bear this punishment than give him away? Well, after all — only one kind ever pities its own kind.'
sentences.n: يَهُونُ can be read either as a plain statement or, as here, as a bitter rhetorical question. كَوْنُهُ is used as a bare causal conjunction, 'because, seeing that,' a colloquial usage standing in for the fuller classical لِكَوْنِهِ. عَلَيْكِي and تُقِرِّي both carry this text's colloquial extra يـ / dropped نَ on 2nd-person feminine forms, kept as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَيَّ الْعِفْرِيتُ وَقَالَ يَا إِنْسِيُّ وَأَنْتَ مَا تَعْرِفُ هَذِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilayya al-ʿifrītu wa-qāla yā insiyyu wa-anta mā taʿrifu hādhihi
sentences.l: Then the efrit turned to me and said: 'O human — do you not know this one?'
sentences.i: Then the efrit turned to me and said, 'You, human — do you truly not know this woman?'
sentences.n: يَا إِنْسِيُّ, 'O human [one],' a nisba noun from إِنْس, 'humankind' — the jinn's own term for marking the narrator as of a different kind from himself, picked up again below (S19).

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ وَمَنْ تَكُونُ هَذِهِ وَمَا رَأَيْتُهَا قَطُّ إِلَّا فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu wa-man takūnu hādhihi wa-mā raʾaytuhā qaṭṭu illā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: So I said: 'And who is this? I have never seen her at all except in this very hour.'
sentences.i: So I said, 'And who is she? I have never laid eyes on her before this very hour.'

sentences.t: قَالَ فَخُذْ هَذَا السَّيْفَ وَاِضْرِبْ عُنُقَهَا وَأَنَا أُطْلِقُكَ تَرُوحُ وَلَا أُنَكِّدُ عَلَيْكَ وَإِنِّي أَتَحَقَّقُ أَنَّكَ لَا تَعْرِفُهَا أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: qāla fa-khudh hādhā al-sayfa wa-iḍrib ʿunuqahā wa-anā uṭliqka tarūḥu wa-lā unakkidu ʿalayka wa-innī ataḥaqqaqu annaka lā taʿrifuhā abadan
sentences.l: He said: 'Then take this sword and strike her neck, and I will release you — you will go free — and I will not trouble you, for indeed I am certain that you do not know her at all.'
sentences.i: He said: 'Then take this sword and strike off her neck, and I will set you free to go your way, and I will trouble you no further — for I am certain you do not know her at all.'
sentences.n: تَرُوحُ, literally 'you go/depart,' stands loosely apposed to أُطْلِقُكَ ('I release you') with no connective — 'I release you, [so that] you go free.'

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ نَعَمْ وَأَخَذْتُ السَّيْفَ وَتَقَدَّمْتُ بِنَشَاطٍ وَرَفَعْتُ يَدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu naʿam wa-akhadhtu al-sayfa wa-taqaddamtu bi-nashāṭin wa-rafaʿtu yadī
sentences.l: So I said, 'Yes,' and I took the sword, and I stepped forward with vigor, and I raised my hand,
sentences.i: So I said, 'Yes,' took up the sword, stepped forward eagerly, and raised my hand,
sentences.n: بِنَشَاطٍ, 'with vigor,' is a بِـ of manner/circumstance (‘forward, [and I did so] with vigor’).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي بِحَاجِبِهَا أَيْ مَا قَصَّرْتُ مَعَكَ أَهَكَذَا تُقَابِلُنِي فَفَهِمْتُ مَا قَالَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī bi-ḥājibihā ay mā qaṣṣartu maʿaka a-hakadhā tuqābilunī fa-fahimtu mā qālat
sentences.l: and she said to me with her eyebrow — that is: 'Have I fallen short with you? Is this how you meet me?' — and I understood what she said,
sentences.i: and with a look of her eyebrow she seemed to say, 'Have I ever failed you, that you should treat me like this?' And I understood her meaning,
sentences.n: بِحَاجِبِهَا, 'with her eyebrow,' names a silent, meaningful gesture; أَيْ that follows introduces the paraphrase of what the gesture meant, 'that is to say.'

sentences.t: وَأَشَرْتُ إِلَيْهَا بِعَيْنِي أَنِّي سَأَفْدِيكِ بِرُوحِي
sentences.tr: wa-asharttu ilayhā bi-ʿaynī annī sa-afdīki bi-rūḥī
sentences.l: and I signaled to her with my eye that I would ransom you with my soul.
sentences.i: and I signaled to her with a glance that I would give my very life to ransom her.
sentences.n: The report slides from third person ('her') into direct address ('I will ransom YOU') within the same clause — the gesture is given as if quoting the very message it silently carried to her.

sentences.t: فَكَتَبَ لِسَانُ حَالِنَا حَيْثُ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-kataba lisānu ḥālinā ḥaythu yaqūlu
sentences.l: So the tongue of our condition wrote, where it says:
sentences.i: And the very tongue of our condition composed these lines, as it says:
sentences.n: لِسَانُ حَالِنَا, 'the tongue of our state,' is an idiom for what one's outward condition silently ‘speaks’ — used to introduce verses voicing feeling neither of them said aloud.

sentences.t:
كَمْ عَاشِقٍ حَلَّتْ بِأَجْفَانِهِ * مَعْشُوقُهُ بِالَّذِي أَضْمَرَا
أَوْحَى إِلَيْهِ لَحْظٌ بِالْعَيْنِ أَنِّي * عَالِمَةٌ بِالَّذِي قَدْ جَرَى
فَمَا اَحْسَنَ اللَّحْظَ فِي وَجْهِهِ * وَمَا اَرْشَقَ الطَّرْفَ اِذْ عَبَرَا
فَهَـٰذَا بِاَجْفَانِهِ كَاتِبٌ * وَذَاكَ بِمُقْلَتِهِ قَدْ قَرَا
sentences.tr:
kam ʿāshiqin ḥallat bi-ajfānihi * maʿshūquhu bi-alladhī aḍmarā
awḥā ilayhi laḥẕun bi-al-ʿayni annī * ʿālimatun bi-alladhī qad jarā
fa-mā aḥsana al-laḥẕa fī wajhihi * wa-mā arshaqa al-ṭarfa idh ʿabarā
fa-hādhā bi-ajfānihi kātibun * wa-dhāka bi-muqlatihi qad qarā
sentences.l:
How many a lover — his beloved has settled in his eyelids, with what she concealed!
A glance of the eye revealed to him that I — * — am one who knows well what has happened.
How fair was the glance in his face! * And how graceful was the look, as it passed by!
So this one is a writer with his eyelids, * and that one has read with his eye's pupil.
sentences.i:
How many a lover has had his beloved settle into his very eyelids, along with all she tried to hide!
A glance of the eye told him — I am one * who knows well all that has passed.
How lovely was the glance on his face, * and how graceful the look, as it swept by!
So one of them wrote with the blink of an eyelid, * and the other read the message with a glance.
sentences.n: Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be; the pointing is the edition's own — including its three unpointed function-words (اَحْسَنَ, اَرْشَقَ, اِذْ), which the archive itself already marks with a bare vowel, so nothing further is supplied. The closing conceit — one lover 'writing' with a glance of the eyelids, the other 'reading' it with a look — caps the poem's theme and directly frames the wordless exchange of glances just described between the narrator and the princess (S8–S9 above).

sentences.t: قَالَ فَهَمَلَتْ عَيْنَايَ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَرَمَيْتُ السَّيْفَ مِنْ يَدِي وَقُلْتُ أَيُّهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ الشَّدِيدُ وَالْبَطَلُ الصِّنْدِيدُ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-hamalat ʿaynāya bi-al-dumūʿi wa-ramaytu al-sayfa min yadī wa-qultu ayyuhā al-ʿifrītu al-shadīdu wa-al-baṭalu al-ṣindīdu
sentences.l: He said: 'Then my two eyes streamed with tears, and I threw the sword from my hand, and I said: O mighty efrit, O formidable champion,
sentences.i: He said: 'Then my eyes ran with tears, and I flung the sword from my hand, and cried: O mighty efrit, O redoubtable champion,

sentences.t: إِذَا كَانَتْ اِمْرَأَةٌ نَاقِصَةُ عَقْلٍ وَدِينٍ مَا اِسْتَحَلَّتْ ضَرْبَ عُنُقِي فَكَيْفَ يَحِلُّ لِي أَنْ أَضْرِبَ عُنُقَهَا وَلَمْ أَرَهَا عُمْرِي
sentences.tr: idhā kānat imraʾatun nāqiṣatu ʿaqlin wa-dīnin mā istaḥallat ḍarba ʿunuqī fa-kayfa yaḥillu lī an aḍriba ʿunuqahā wa-lam arahā ʿumrī
sentences.l: If a woman deficient in reason and religion did not deem lawful the striking of my neck, then how should it be lawful for me that I strike her neck, when I have never seen her in my life?
sentences.i: If even a woman — deficient as she is in reason and religion — did not see fit to take my life, how then could it be right for me to take hers, when I have never once set eyes on her before?
sentences.n: اِمْرَأَةٌ is spelled with its hamza already precomposed in the archive (kept, per the rule for a hamza the edition itself prints), unlike most of the other hamzas in this slice. نَاقِصَةُ عَقْلٍ وَدِينٍ, 'deficient in reason and religion,' echoes the well-known hadith description of women — the narrator turns the commonplace into an a fortiori argument for his own innocence.

sentences.t: فَلَا أَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ أَبَدًا وَلَوْ سُقِيتُ كَأْسَ الْمَوْتِ وَالرَّدَى
sentences.tr: fa-lā afʿalu dhālika abadan wa-law suqītu kaʾsa al-mawti wa-al-radā
sentences.l: So I will not do that, ever, even if I were made to drink the cup of death and destruction.
sentences.i: So I will never do such a thing, though I be made to drink the very cup of death and ruin.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ أَنْتُمَا تَعْرِفَا صَنِيعَةً بَيْنَكُمَا أَنَا أُرِيكُمَا عَاقِبَةَ فِعَالِكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu antumā taʿrifā ṣanīʿatan baynakumā anā urīkumā ʿāqibata fiʿālikumā
sentences.l: Then the efrit said: 'You two know some deed between you; I will show you two the consequence of your doings.'
sentences.i: The efrit said: 'The two of you know full well what has passed between you — now I will show you both the price of your deeds.'
sentences.n: تَعْرِفَا drops the classical dual ending's final نِ (تَعْرِفَانِ) — another of this narrative's Middle Arabic dual forms, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ الْعِفْرِيتُ السَّيْفَ وَضَرَبَ يَدَ الصَّبِيَّةِ قَطَعَهَا ثُمَّ ضَرَبَ الثَّانِيَةَ قَطَعَهَا فَقَطَعَ أَرْبَعَتَهَا بِأَرْبَعِ ضَرَبَاتٍ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha al-ʿifrītu al-sayfa wa-ḍaraba yada al-ṣabiyyati qaṭaʿahā thumma ḍaraba al-thāniyata qaṭaʿahā fa-qaṭaʿa arbaʿatahā bi-arbaʿi ḍarabātin
sentences.l: So the efrit took the sword, and struck the young woman's hand, severing it; then he struck the second, severing it; so he cut off her four with four blows.
sentences.i: So the efrit seized the sword and struck at the young woman's hand, hewing it off; then struck the other, hewing it off too — so with four strokes he cut off all four of her limbs.
sentences.n: أَرْبَعَتَهَا, 'her four,' apparently refers to all four of her limbs (both hands and both feet), though only two strikes to her hands are actually named before this tally — the compression is the text's own, kept as printed rather than spelled out.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَنْظُرُ وَأَيْقَنْتُ بِالْمَوْتِ وَقَدْ أَشَارَتْ أَشَارَتْ إِلَيَّ بِعَيْنِهَا كَالْمُوَدِّعِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā anẕuru wa-ayqantu bi-al-mawti wa-qad ashārat ashārat ilayya bi-ʿaynihā ka-al-muwaddiʿi
sentences.l: while I looked on, and I was certain of death; and she gestured — gestured to me with her eye, like the one taking leave.
sentences.i: and I looked on, certain that death had come for me; and she gave me one last look, like someone bidding farewell.
sentences.n: أَشَارَتْ أَشَارَتْ repeats the same verb twice with no connective — almost certainly the compositor's dittography rather than a deliberate doubling (contrast the genuine intensifying doublets elsewhere in the Nights, e.g. فُحِّمَ سُوِّدَ), kept here exactly as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ قَالَ لَهَا زَنَيْتِي بِعَيْنِكِ وَضَرَبَهَا طَيَّرَ رَاسَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿifrīta qāla lahā zanaytī bi-ʿaynika wa-ḍarabahā ṭayyara rāsahā
sentences.l: Then indeed the efrit said to her: 'You committed adultery with your eye!' And he struck her, making her head fly off.
sentences.i: Then the efrit said to her, 'You played the harlot with your very eye!' — and he struck her, and her head went flying.
sentences.n: زَنَيْتِ بِعَيْنِكِ, 'you committed adultery with your eye,' treats the wordless exchange of glances just described (S8–S9, S11) as an act of betrayal in itself. رَاسَهَا keeps this text's colloquial spelling of رَأْسَهَا, 'her head' — the hamza consonant genuinely unpronounced in this form, as already met in رَاسَكَ earlier in the qalandar's tale.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ يَا إِنْسِيُّ نَحْنُ فِي شَرْعِنَا إِذَا زَنَتِ الزَّوْجَةُ يَحِلُّ لَنَا قَتْلُهَا
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilayya wa-qāla yā insiyyu naḥnu fī sharʿinā idhā zanati al-zawjatu yaḥillu lanā qatluhā
sentences.l: Then he turned to me and said: 'O human, in our law, if the wife commits adultery, the killing of her is lawful for us.'
sentences.i: Then he turned to me and said, 'Listen, human — under our law, if a wife is unfaithful, it is lawful for us to kill her.'

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةُ خَطَفْتُهَا لَيْلَةَ عُرْسِهَا وَهِيَ بِنْتُ اِثْنَىْ عَشَرَ سَنَةً وَلَمْ تَعْرِفْ أَحَدًا غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi al-ṣabiyyatu khaṭaftuhā laylata ʿursihā wa-hiya bintu ithnay ʿashara sanatan wa-lam taʿrif aḥadan ghayrī
sentences.l: And this young woman — I snatched her on the night of her wedding, when she was a girl of twelve years, and she knew no one but me.
sentences.i: As for this girl — I carried her off on her very wedding night, when she was but a child of twelve, and she has known no one in this world but me.
sentences.n: اِثْنَيْ عَشَرَ keeps the masculine numeral form though سَنَةً is feminine — Classical grammar would want اثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً — another instance of this text's loose gender agreement with compound numerals (cf. الثَّانِيَةَ عَشَرَ in Night 12's opening formula).

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ أَجِيءُ عِنْدَهَا فِي كُلِّ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ لَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً وَكُنْتُ أَجِيئُهَا فِى زِيِّ رَجُلٍ عَجَمِيٍّ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu ajīʾu ʿindahā fī kulli ʿasharati ayyāmin laylatan wāḥidatan wa-kuntu ajīʾuhā fī ziyyi rajulin ʿajamiyyin
sentences.l: And I used to come to her, every ten days, one night; and I used to come to her in the guise of a foreign man.
sentences.i: I would visit her once every ten days, for a single night, coming to her in the dress of a foreign man.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَحَقَّقْتُ أَنَّهَا خَانَتْنِي قَتَلْتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taḥaqqaqtu annahā khānatnī qataltuhā
sentences.l: So when I ascertained that she had betrayed me, I killed her.
sentences.i: So when I was certain she had betrayed me, I killed her.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَنْتَ فَلَمْ أَتَحَقَّقْ أَنَّكَ خُنْتَنِي فِيهَا وَلَٰكِنْ لَابُدَّ أَنِّي مَا أُخْلِيكَ فِي عَافِيَةٍ فَتَمَنَّ عَلَىَّ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā anta fa-lam ataḥaqqaq annaka khuntanī fīhā wa-lākin lā budda annī mā ukhlīka fī ʿāfiyatin fa-tamanna ʿalayya
sentences.l: As for you, I did not ascertain that you had wronged me regarding her; but it must be that I will not leave you unharmed — so make your wish of me.
sentences.i: As for you, though, I could never be certain you had wronged me through her; but still, I cannot let you go scot-free — so tell me what you wish.
sentences.n: أُخْلِيكَ فِي عَافِيَةٍ, literally 'leave you in soundness,' idiomatically 'leave you unharmed, let you off.' تَمَنَّ عَلَيَّ here means less 'make a wish' than 'choose, state a preference' — as the efrit's next words make clear, the only choice on offer is among forms of punishment.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحْتُ يَا سَيِّدَتِي غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ وَقُلْتُ وَمَا وَمَا أَتَمَنَّاءْ عَلَيْكَ عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥtu yā sayyidatī ghāyata al-faraḥi wa-qultu wa-mā wa-mā atamannāʾ ʿalayka ʿalayka
sentences.l: So I rejoiced, O my lady, with the utmost joy, and I said: 'And what — and what should I wish of you, of you?'
sentences.i: I rejoiced, O my lady, with the utmost joy, and said, 'And what should I wish from you?'
sentences.n: The archive prints وَمَا وَمَا ... عَلَيْكَ عَلَيْكَ with 'and what' and 'of you' each doubled, and an extra ء tacked onto اتمنى (expected أَتَمَنَّى, 'I wish' — the ا for ى is an ordinary variant spelling, but the trailing ء has no root to attach to). This reads as simple compositor's dittography rather than a deliberate repetition (cf. أَشَارَتْ أَشَارَتْ above and طَمِعْتُ طَمِعْتُ below), kept letter for letter and vocalized by evident sense.

sentences.t: قَالَ تَمَنَّ عَلَىَّ أَيَّ صُورَةٍ أَسْحَرُكَ فِيهَا إِمَّا صُورَةَ كَلْبٍ أَوْ حِمَارٍ أَوْ قِرْدٍ
sentences.tr: qāla tamanna ʿalayya ayya ṣūratin asḥaruka fīhā immā ṣūrata kalbin aw ḥimārin aw qirdin
sentences.l: He said: 'Propose to me: in whichever form I should enchant you — either the form of a dog, or a donkey, or a monkey.'
sentences.i: He answered: 'Choose, then, what shape I shall put a spell on you into — a dog, say, or a donkey, or an ape.'
sentences.n: أَيَّ صُورَةٍ ... إِمَّا ... أَوْ ... أَوْ, 'in whichever form — either... or... or,' makes plain that the 'wish' on offer is not release but only a choice among forms of animal transformation.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ وَقَدْ طَمِعْتُ طَمِعْتُ أَنَّهُ يَعْفُو عَنِّي وَاللَّهِ إِنْ عَفَوْتَ عَنِّي يَعْفُ اللَّهُ عَنْكَ بِعَفْوِكَ عَنْ رَجُلٍ مُسْلِمٍ لَمْ يُؤْذِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu wa-qad ṭamiʿtu ṭamiʿtu annahu yaʿfū ʿannī wa-Allāhi in ʿafawta ʿannī yaʿfu Allāhu ʿanka bi-ʿafwika ʿan rajulin muslimin lam yuʾdhika
sentences.l: So I said — having hoped, hoped that he would pardon me — 'By God, if you pardon me, God will pardon you, for your pardoning a Muslim man who has not harmed you.'
sentences.i: So I said, hoping against hope that he would spare me: 'By God, if you pardon me, God will pardon you, for showing mercy to a Muslim man who has never done you harm.'
sentences.n: طَمِعْتُ طَمِعْتُ, 'I hoped, I hoped,' is again printed twice with no connective — kept as printed rather than silently reduced to one (cf. أَشَارَتْ أَشَارَتْ above). بِعَفْوِكَ: the بِـ names the ground/cause for which God will pardon him — 'for/on account of your pardoning...'.

sentences.t: وَتَضَرَّعْتُ غَايَةَ التَّضَرُّعِ وَبَقِيتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ أَنَا مَظْلُومٌ
sentences.tr: wa-taḍarraʿtu ghāyata al-taḍarruʿi wa-baqītu bayna yadayhi wa-qultu lahu anā maẕlūmun
sentences.l: And I implored most earnestly, and I remained before him, and I said to him: 'I am wronged.'
sentences.i: And I begged and pleaded with all my might, staying humbled before him, and said, 'I am a man wronged.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَا تُطِلْ عَلَيَّ الْكَلَامَ مَا يَبْعَلُ عَلَيَّ قَتْلُكَ وَلَٰكِنْ أُخَيِّرُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā tuṭil ʿalayya al-kalāma mā yabʿalu ʿalayya qatluka wa-lākin ukhayyiruka
sentences.l: So he said: 'Do not prolong speech to me — your killing does not confound me; but I will give you a choice.'
sentences.i: But he said, 'Don't waste words on me — killing you would cost me nothing at all; but I will give you a choice.'
sentences.n: يَبْعَلُ, from بَعِلَ 'to be confounded, at a loss, unable to manage a thing' (so Lane's Lexicon, aor. يَبْعَلُ) — 'your killing does not trouble/confound me,' i.e. it would cost the efrit nothing to kill him. The root is easy to mistake for بَعْل, 'husband, master' (which does not fit here), but the archive's own letters support this direct reading without any emendation.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ أَيُّهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ إِنَّ الْعَفْوَ عَنِّي هُوَ أَلْيَقُ بِكَ فَاُعْفُ عَنِّي كَمَا عَفَا الْمَحْسُودُ عَنِ الْحَاسِدِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu ayyuhā al-ʿifrītu inna al-ʿafwa ʿannī huwa alyaqu bika fa-uʿfu ʿannī kamā ʿafā al-maḥsūdu ʿani al-ḥāsidi
sentences.l: So I said: 'O efrit, indeed pardon for me is more fitting for you; so pardon me, as al-Maḥsūd pardoned al-Ḩāsid.'
sentences.i: So I said, 'O efrit, mercy toward me becomes you far better than vengeance; so pardon me, just as the Envied Man pardoned the Envier.'
sentences.n: الْمَحْسُودُ ('the Envied') and الْحَاسِدُ ('the Envier') are the title characters of the embedded tale the narrator is about to tell as a precedent for mercy — not yet narrated in this slice, only invoked here by name.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ وَكَيْفَ كَانَ ذَلِكَ فَقُلْتُ زَعَمُوا أَيُّهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ أَنَّهُ؛
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu wa-kayfa kāna dhālika fa-qultu zaʿamū ayyuhā al-ʿifrītu annahu;
sentences.l: So the efrit said, ‘And how was that?’ So I said: ‘It is said, O Efrit, that —
sentences.i: Then the efrit said, ‘And how did that happen?’ So I said, ‘They say, O Efrit, that —
sentences.n: زَعَمُوا, 'it is claimed, they allege,' is the impersonal formula opening a tale-within-a-tale. The Second Qalandar — still speaking to the efrit that threatens him within his own frame-tale — now tells this separate story of the Envied Man and the Envier, hoping it will move the efrit to mercy.

sentences.t: كَانَ رَجُلَانِ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ سَاكِنَيْنِ فِى بَيْتَيْنِ بِحَائِطٍ وَاحِدٍ مُلْصَقَيْنِ وَكَانَ وَاحِدُهُمَا يَحْسُدُ الْأخَرَ وَيُصِيبُهُ بِعَيْنِهِ وَيُبَالِغُ فِي أَذِيَّتِهِ وَكُلَّ وَقْتٍ يَحْسُدُ؛
sentences.tr: kāna rajulāni fī al-madīnati sākinayni fī baytayni bi-ḥāʾiṭin wāḥidin mulṣaqayni wa-kāna wāḥiduhumā yaḥsudu al-ākhara wa-yuṣībuhu bi-ʿaynihi wa-yubālighu fī adhiyyatihi wa-kulla waqtin yaḥsudu;
sentences.l: There were two men in the city, dwelling in two houses joined by a single wall, adjoining; and one of them used to envy the other, and strike him with his [evil] eye, and go to excess in molesting him — and at every moment he envied;
sentences.i: There were once two men in the city who lived in two houses joined by a single shared wall; and one of them was forever envying the other, casting the evil eye upon him, and going to great lengths to torment him — envying him every moment;
sentences.n: سَاكِنَيْنِ and مُلْصَقَيْنِ both print the dual ending ـين (accusative/genitive) where Classical grammar, agreeing with the nominative dual رَجُلَانِ as predicate of كَانَ, would call for the nominative dual ـَانِ — the same loose government of كان met elsewhere in this Middle Arabic prose. بِعَيْنِهِ, 'with his eye,' refers to the evil eye (al-ʿayn), a real and widely feared power of an envious gaze.

sentences.t: وَزَادَ بِهِ حَسَدٌ؛ حَتَّى أَنَّهُ قَلَّلَ فِى طَعَامِهِ وَلَذِيذِ مَنَامِهِ وَالْمَحْسُودُ لَا يَزْدَادُ إِلَّا خَيْرًا وَكُلَّمَا تَغَلَّبَ فِيهِ زَادَ وَنَمَا وَذَكَا
sentences.tr: wa-zāda bihi ḥasadun; ḥattā annahu qallala fī ṭaʿāmihi wa-ladhīdhi manāmihi wa-al-maḥsūdu lā yazdādu illā khayran wa-kullamā taghallaba fīhi zāda wa-namā wa-dhakā
sentences.l: And envy toward him increased; until he lessened his food, and [in] the sweetness of his sleep. But the envied man increased in nothing but good, and the more it prevailed against him, the more he grew, and throve, and blazed the brighter.
sentences.i: And his neighbor's envy of him only grew, until he stinted his food and the sweetness of his sleep. Yet the envied man throve in nothing but good; the more envy got the better of him, the more he grew, flourished, and shone the brighter.
sentences.n: ذَكَا can mean either 'grew sharp-witted, clever' or, of a fire, 'blazed up, burned brighter' — the ambiguity is kept, since either fits the point that the envied man only thrived under his neighbor's malice.

sentences.t: فَبَلَغَ الْمَحْسُودَ حَسَدُهُ جَارُهُ لَهُ وَأَذِيَّتُهُ لَهُ فَرَحَلَ مِنْ جِوَارِهِ وَأَبْعَدَ عَنْ أَرْضِهِ وَقَالَ وَاللَّهِ لَأَهْجُرَنَّ الدُّنْيَا لِأَجْلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-balagha al-maḥsūda ḥasaduhu jāruhu lahu wa-adhiyyatuhu lahu fa-raḥala min jiwārihi wa-abʿada ʿan arḍihi wa-qāla wa-Allāhi la-ahjuranna al-dunyā li-ajlihi
sentences.l: So there reached the envied man the envying of him — his neighbor — toward him, and his molestation of him; so he moved away from his neighborhood and went far from his land, and said, 'By God, I will surely forsake the world on his account!'
sentences.i: Word of his neighbor's envy and persecution at last reached the envied man, so he moved away from his neighborhood and went far from his homeland, saying, 'By God, I will leave this place forever because of him!'
sentences.n: حَسَدُهُ جَارُهُ لَهُ piles up subject and appositive rather loosely — 'his envying of him, [namely] his neighbor, toward him' — evidently meaning simply 'his neighbor's envy of him,' with the pronoun on حَسَدُهُ anticipating جَارُهُ, a paratactic habit typical of this Middle Arabic prose. الدُّنْيَا, literally 'the world,' stands here as elsewhere for one's present home or life — 'to forsake the world for his sake' means simply to leave that land because of him.

sentences.t: وَسَكَنَ فِي مَدِينَةٍ أُخْرَى وَاشْتَرَى لَهُ فِيهَا أَرْضًا وَكَانَ فِي تِلْكَ الْأَرْضِ بِئْرٌ سَاقِيَةٌ قَدِيمَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-sakana fī madīnatin ukhrā wa-ishtarā lahu fīhā arḍan wa-kāna fī tilka al-arḍi biʾrun sāqiyatun qadīmatun
sentences.l: And he settled in another city, and bought for himself land there; and in that land was an old draw-well.
sentences.i: He settled in another city and bought himself a plot of land there; and on that land stood an old draw-well.
sentences.n: بِئْرٌ سَاقِيَةٌ, literally 'a well, a water-drawing one,' is a well fitted for drawing water, rendered simply 'a draw-well.'

sentences.t: وَعَمَّرَ لَهُ بِهَا زَاوِيَةً وَاشْتَرَى لَهُ كُلَّ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهَا وَعَبَدَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى فِيهَا وَأَخْلَصَ عِبَادَتَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿammara lahu bihā zāwiyatan wa-ishtarā lahu kulla mā yaḥtāju ilayhā wa-ʿabada Allāha taʿālā fīhā wa-akhlaṣa ʿibādatahu
sentences.l: And he built for himself there a hermitage, and bought for himself all that it needed, and worshipped God, Most High, therein, and made his worship sincere.
sentences.i: There he built himself a hermitage, bought everything it required, and gave himself to worshipping God Most High within it, wholly devoted in his devotion.
sentences.n: زَاوِيَة, 'hermitage, retreat' — literally 'a corner' — is the standard term for a small lodge where a holy man lives and gathers disciples; it recurs throughout this tale.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتْهُ الْفُقَرَاءُ وَالْمَسَاكِينُ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ وَ شَاعَ خَبَرُهُ فِي تِلْكَ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾathu al-fuqarāʾu wa-al-masākīnu min kulli jānibin wa-shāʿa khabaruhu fī tilka al-madīnati
sentences.l: And the poor and the destitute came to him from every side, and his fame spread abroad in that city.
sentences.i: The poor and the destitute flocked to him from every quarter, and word of him spread throughout that city.
sentences.n: جَاءَتْهُ agrees in the feminine singular with الْفُقَرَاءُ alone though a compound subject follows (الفقراء والمساكين) — another instance of this text's loose subject–verb agreement.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اتَّصَلَ خَبَرُهُ بِجَارِهِ الْحَاسِدِ لَهُ بِمَا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الْخَيْرِ وَسَارُوا يَقْصُدُونَ إِلَيْهِ أَكَابِرُ الْمَدِينَةِ فَدَخَلَ الزَّاوِيَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma ittaṣala khabaruhu bi-jārihi al-ḥāsidi lahu bimā waṣala ilayhi mina al-khayri wa-sārū yaqṣudūna ilayhi akābiru al-madīnati fa-dakhala al-zāwiyata
sentences.l: Then news of him reached his envious neighbor, of the good that had come to him; and the great ones of the city journeyed, making for him; so he entered the hermitage.
sentences.i: Then his envious neighbor came to hear of the good fortune that had befallen him; and the notables of the city set out, making their way to him — and so the envier, too, entered the hermitage.
sentences.n: سَارُوا يَقْصُدُونَ إِلَيْهِ أَكَابِرُ الْمَدِينَةِ places the verb and its pronoun subject (سَارُوا) before the noun that actually names the subject (أَكَابِرُ الْمَدِينَةِ, 'the notables of the city') — a delayed-subject construction typical of this narrative style. فَدَخَلَ, 'so he entered,' returns to the envious neighbor as subject, resuming the main thread of the story.

sentences.t: فَتَلَقَّاهُ؛ الْجَارُ الْمَحْسُودُ بِالرَّحْبِ وَالسَّعَةِ وَأَكْرَمَهُ غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-talaqqāhu; al-jāru al-maḥsūdu bi-al-raḥbi wa-al-saʿati wa-akramahu ghāyata al-ikrāmi
sentences.l: So he was met — the envied neighbor — with welcome and ampleness, and he honored him with the utmost of honoring.
sentences.i: The envied neighbor met him with open welcome, and showed him the greatest honor.
sentences.n: The archive's own semicolon falls oddly mid-clause, right after the verb and before its subject (الْجَارُ الْمَحْسُودُ) — kept exactly as printed. غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ is a cognate-type accusative of emphasis, 'honored him [to] the utmost of honoring.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْحَاسِدُ لِي مَعَكَ كَلَامٌ وَهُوَ سَبَبُ سَفَرِي إِلَيْكَ وَأُرِيدُ أُبَشِّرُلَكَ فَقُمْ وَامْشِ مَعِي فِي زَاوِيَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ḥāsidu lī maʿaka kalāmun wa-huwa sababu safarī ilayka wa-urīdu ubashshirulaka fa-qum wa-imshi maʿī fī zāwiyatika
sentences.l: So the envier said to him, 'I have a word with you, and it is the reason for my journey to you, and I want — I bring-you-good-news — so arise, and walk with me in your hermitage.'
sentences.i: Then the envier said to him, 'I have something to say to you, which is the very reason for my journey to you, and I want to give you good news — so get up, and walk with me a way into your hermitage.'
sentences.n: أُبَشِّرُلَكَ prints أُبَشِّرُ, 'I give glad tidings,' fused directly onto لَكَ, 'to you,' with no space and no أَنْ linking it to أُرِيدُ — a colloquial construction (وأريد + bare present verb, without the subjunctive أَنْ a Classical register would require), kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْمَحْسُودُ وَأَخَذَ بِيَدِ الْحَاسِدِ وَ تَمَشَّوْا إِلَى آخِرِ الزَّاوِيَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-maḥsūdu wa-akhadha bi-yadi al-ḥāsidi wa-tamashshaw ilā ākhiri al-zāwiyati
sentences.l: So the envied man arose, and took the envier by the hand, and the two of them walked to the far end of the hermitage.
sentences.i: So the envied man got up, took the envier by the hand, and the two of them walked on to the far end of the hermitage.
sentences.n: تَمَشَّوْا, 'they walked,' takes the sound plural ending though only two men are meant — Classical grammar would call for the dual تَمَشَّيَا, another instance of this text's loose number agreement.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَاسِدُ قُلْ لِفُقَرَائِكَ يَدْخُلُونَ إِلَى خَلَوَاتِهِمْ فَأَنَا مَا أَقُولُ لَكَ إِلَّا سِرًّا بِحَيْثُ لَا أَحَدٌ يَسْمَعُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥāsidu qul li-fuqarāʾika yadkhulūna ilā khalawātihim fa-anā mā aqūlu laka illā sirran bi-ḥaythu lā aḥadun yasmaʿunā
sentences.l: So the envier said, 'Tell your poor-brethren to go into their cells, for I — I will say to you nothing but in secret, in such a way that no one hears us.'
sentences.i: Then the envier said, 'Tell your poor brethren to go into their cells, for I will speak to you only in private, where no one can overhear us.'
sentences.n: يَدْخُلُونَ carries an implied imperative sense ('let them go in') though it is grammatically a plain indicative — a command given without a jussive, common in this narrative style.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَحْسُودُ لِفُقَرَائِهِ ادْخُلُوا إِلَى خَلَوَاتِكُمْ فَفَعَلُوا كَمَا أَمَرَهُم بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maḥsūdu li-fuqarāʾihi udkhulū ilā khalawātikum fa-faʿalū kamā amarahum bihi
sentences.l: So the envied man said to his poor-brethren, 'Go into your cells.' So they did as he had commanded them with it.
sentences.i: So the envied man said to his poor brethren, 'Go to your cells.' And they did as he had bidden them.

sentences.t: وَمَشَى بِهِ قَلِيلًا إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَ بِهِ إِلَى الْبِئْرِ الْقَدِيمِ
sentences.tr: wa-mashā bihi qalīlan ilā an waṣala bihi ilā al-biʾri al-qadīmi
sentences.l: And he walked with him a little way, until he brought him to the old well.
sentences.i: Then he walked on with him a short way, until he had brought him to the old well.

sentences.t: فَدَفَعَ الْحَاسِدُ الْمَحْسُودَ فَأَلْقَاهُ فِي الْبِئْرِ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِهِ أَحَدٌ وَخَرَجَ وَرَاحَ فِي سَبِيلِهِ وَظَنَّ أَنَّهُ قَتَلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-dafaʿa al-ḥāsidu al-maḥsūda fa-alqāhu fī al-biʾri wa-lam yaʿlam bihi aḥadun wa-kharaja wa-rāḥa fī sabīlihi wa-ẕanna annahu qatalahu
sentences.l: So the envier pushed the envied man, and cast him into the well, and no one knew of it; and he went out and went his way, and thought that he had killed him.
sentences.i: Then the envier pushed the envied man and cast him into the well, and no one knew of it; and he went off about his business, believing he had killed him.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْبِئْرُ مَسْكُونًا مِنَ الْجِنِّ فَالْتَقَطُوهُ قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا وَأَقْعَدُوهُ عَلَى الصَّخْرَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-biʾru maskūnan mina al-jinni fa-iltaqaṭūhu qalīlan qalīlan wa-aqʿadūhu ʿalā al-ṣakhrati
sentences.l: Now the well was inhabited by the jinn; so they gathered him up little by little, and seated him upon the rock.
sentences.i: Now the well was home to the jinn, and they caught him as he fell, little by little, and set him down safely upon a rock.
sentences.n: قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا, literally 'a little, a little,' idiomatically 'bit by bit' — the jinn breaking his fall gradually rather than letting him strike the bottom.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ لِبَعْضٍ تَعْرِفُونَ مَنْ هَذَا قَالُوا لَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍin taʿrifūna man hādhā qālū lā
sentences.l: And some of them said to others, 'Do you know who this is?' They said, 'No.'

sentences.t: قَالَ قَائِلٌ مِنْهُمْ هَذَا الرَّجُلُ الْمَحْسُودُ الَّذِي هَرَبَ مِنْ حَاسِدِهِ وَسَكَنَ مَدِينَتَنَا وَأَنْشَأَ هَذِهِ الزَّاوِيَةَ وَآنَسَنَا بِذِكْرِهِ وَقِرَاءَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla qāʾilun minhum hādhā al-rajulu al-maḥsūdu alladhī haraba min ḥāsidihi wa-sakana madīnatanā wa-anshaʾa hādhihi al-zāwiyata wa-ānasanā bi-dhikrihi wa-qirāʾatihi
sentences.l: A speaker among them said, 'This is the envied man, the one who fled from his envier, and settled in our city, and built this hermitage, and has cheered us with his remembrance [of God] and his recitation.'
sentences.i: One of them spoke up and said, 'This is the envied man — the one who fled his envier, settled in our city, built this very hermitage, and has been good company to us with his devotions and his recitation.'
sentences.n: بِذِكْرِهِ وَقِرَاءَتِهِ, 'with his remembrance and his recitation,' refers to his dhikr (repeated invocation of God) and his Qur'ān recitation — the two devotions that had made him welcome company for the jinn of the well.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَافَرَ لَهُ الْحَاسِدُ حَتَّى اجْتَمَعَ بِهِ وَتَحَيَّلَ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّى رَمَاهُ عَنْكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qad sāfara lahu al-ḥāsidu ḥattā ijtamaʿa bihi wa-taḥayyala ʿalayhi ḥattā ramāhu ʿankum
sentences.l: And his envier had journeyed to him, until he came together with him, and schemed against him, until he cast him down — away from you.
sentences.i: His envier had journeyed to find him, until he had met with him, and worked a trick upon him, until he flung him down — here among you.
sentences.n: عَنْكُمْ, 'away from you' (pl.), is puzzling in the mouth of one jinni speaking to fellow jinn about a third party; it may be a slip for عِنْدَكُمْ, 'at your place, here where you are' (i.e. down the well, among the jinn themselves), which would make plain sense of the scene — kept as printed and rendered by that likelier sense.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اتَّصَلَ خَبَرُهُ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ إِلَى سُلْطَانِ هَذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَعَزَمَ عَلَى زِيَارَتِهِ فِي غَلَاةٍ لِأَجْلِ بِنْتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi ittaṣala khabaruhu fī hādhihi al-laylati ilā sulṭāni hādhihi al-madīnati wa-ʿazama ʿalā ziyāratihi fī ghalātin li-ajli bintihi
sentences.l: And news of him has, this very night, reached the sultan of this city, and he has resolved upon visiting him presently, for the sake of his daughter.
sentences.i: And this very night, word of him has reached the sultan of this city, who has resolved to visit him presently, for his daughter's sake.
sentences.n: غَلَاة is an obscure form whose consonants do not cleanly match any common Classical word; it is vocalized here by evident sense and rendered 'presently, shortly.' It may be a corrupt or dialectal form related to غَدَاة, 'early morning' (the king does in fact arrive the next morning, just as dawn breaks, in the lines below) — but no reading is certain, and the word is pointed as printed rather than silently repaired.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ وَ مَا الَّذِي بِابْنَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla baʿḍuhum wa-mā alladhī bi-ibnatihi
sentences.l: So one of them said, 'And what is it that is with his daughter?'
sentences.i: Then one of them said, 'And what ails his daughter?'

sentences.t: قَالَ بِهَا جُنُونٌ وَقَدْ تَوَلَّعَ بِهَا جُنُونُ مَيْمُونَ بْنِ دَمْلَمَ
sentences.tr: qāla bihā junūnun wa-qad tawallaʿa bihā junūnu Maymūna bni Damlama
sentences.l: He said, 'Upon her is madness; and indeed the madness of Maymūn son of Damlam has become fastened upon her.'
sentences.i: He said, 'She is afflicted with madness — the madness of Maymūn son of Damlam has taken hold of her.'
sentences.n: Maymūn ibn Damlam is named as though a known figure — apparently a jinni or demon-king whose particular madness/possession is meant, in the way this literature often attaches such afflictions to a named jinni; the spelling دملم is kept exactly as printed, with no attempt to normalize it to some better-known form.

sentences.t: وَلَوْ عَرَفَ دَوَاءَهَا لَكَانَ أَبْرَأَهَا وَدَوَاءُهَا أَهْوَنُ مَا يَكُونُ
sentences.tr: wa-law ʿarafa dawāʾahā la-kāna abraʾahā wa-dawāʾuhā ahwanu mā yakūnu
sentences.l: And had he known her cure, he would have cured her already; and her cure is the easiest thing there could be.
sentences.i: And had he known her cure, he would long since have healed her — yet her cure is the simplest thing imaginable.

sentences.t: قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ وَمَا دَوَاءُهَا
sentences.tr: qāla baʿḍuhum wa-mā dawāʾuhā
sentences.l: One of them said, 'And what is her cure?'

sentences.t: قَالَ الْقِطُّ الْأَسْوَدُ الَّذِي عِنْدَهُ فِي الزَّاوِيَةِ فِي آخِرِ ذَنَبِهِ نُقْطَةٌ بَيْضَاءُ بِقَدْرِ الدِّرْهَمِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-qiṭṭu al-aswadu alladhī ʿindahu fī al-zāwiyati fī ākhiri dhanabihi nuqṭatun bayḍāʾu bi-qadri al-dirhami
sentences.l: He said, 'The black cat that he has at the hermitage — at the end of its tail is a white spot the size of the dirham.'
sentences.i: He said, 'The black cat he keeps at the hermitage has, at the tip of its tail, a white spot the size of a coin.'
sentences.n: الدِّرْهَم, 'the dirham,' a silver coin, is used here simply as a familiar measure of small size.

sentences.t: يَأْخُذُ مِنْهَا سَبْعَ شَعَرَاتٍ مِنَ الشَّعْرِ الْأَبْيَضِ فَيُبَخِّرُهَا بِهَا
sentences.tr: yaʾkhudhu minhā sabʿa shaʿarātin mina al-shaʿri al-abyaḍi fa-yubakhkhiruhā bihā
sentences.l: One takes from it seven hairs of the white fur, and fumigates her with them.
sentences.i: Someone must pluck from it seven hairs of that white fur, and fumigate her with them.

sentences.t: فَيَرُوحُ الْمَارِدُ مِنْ عَلَى رَاسِهَا وَلَا يَعُودُ إِلَيْهَا أَبَدًا وَتَبْرِي لِوَقْتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-yarūḥu al-māridu min ʿalā rāsihā wa-lā yaʿūdu ilayhā abadan wa-tabrī li-waqtihā
sentences.l: Then the demon will depart from off her head, and will never return to her again, and she will be cured at once.
sentences.i: Then the demon will leave her head, and never come back to her, and she will be cured then and there.
sentences.n: رَاسِهَا drops the hamza of Classical رَأْسِهَا, 'her head' — a colloquial spelling met elsewhere in this literature. تَبْرِي is likewise this text's colloquial rendering of Classical تَبْرَأُ, 'she recovers,' its final hamza replaced by a yā’.

sentences.t: أَيُّهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ هَذَا كُلُّهُ جَرَى وَالْمَحْسُودُ يَسْمَعُ
sentences.tr: ayyuhā al-ʿifrītu hādhā kulluhu jarā wa-al-maḥsūdu yasmaʿu
sentences.l: O Efrit, all this happened while the envied man was listening.
sentences.n: The Second Qalandar breaks briefly out of the jinn's own dialogue to address the efrit directly, as at the tale's opening — a reminder that this whole episode is itself being retold to the frame's own efrit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ وَطَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ وَلَاحَ جَاءَ الْفُقَرَاءُ إِلَى الشَّيْخِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu wa-ṭalaʿa al-fajru wa-lāḥa jāʾa al-fuqarāʾu ilā al-shaykhi
sentences.l: So when morning came, and the dawn rose, and shone forth, the poor-brethren came to the shaykh.
sentences.i: So when morning broke, and the dawn rose and shone forth, the poor brethren came to the shaykh.
sentences.n: أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ, 'the morning became morning,' pairs the verb with its own cognate subject for emphasis, echoed again by طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ وَلَاحَ, 'the dawn rose and shone' — a stock triple formula for daybreak.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدُوهُ طَالِعًا مِنَ الْبِئْرِ فَعَظُمَ فِي أَعْيُنِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadūhu ṭāliʿan mina al-biʾri fa-ʿaẕuma fī aʿyunihim
sentences.l: And they found him coming up out of the well; so he grew great in their eyes.
sentences.i: And they found him climbing up out of the well; so he grew great in their eyes.
