sentences.n: فَعَظُمَ فِي أَعْيُنِهِمْ, literally 'he grew great in their eyes,' means his standing rose all the higher in their esteem — his escape from the well seeming to them a miracle.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لِلْمَحْسُودِ دَوَاءٌ إِلَّا الْقِطُّ الْأَسْوَدُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yakun li-al-maḥsūdi dawāʾun illā al-qiṭṭu al-aswadu
sentences.l: And the envied man had no cure but the black cat.
sentences.i: And the envied man's only remedy was the black cat.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ مِنَ النُّقْطَةِ الْبَيْضَاءِ الَّتِي فِي ذَنَبِهِ سَبْعَ شَعَرَاتٍ وَشَالَهُم مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha mina al-nuqṭati al-bayḍāʾi allatī fī dhanabihi sabʿa shaʿarātin wa-shālahum maʿahu
sentences.l: So he took, from the white spot that was on its tail, seven hairs, and carried them with him.
sentences.i: So he took seven hairs from the white spot on its tail, and carried them off with him.
sentences.n: شَالَ, 'to carry, lift,' is a colloquial verb (still current in Egyptian Arabic) standing in for Classical حَمَلَ; kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ إِلَّا وَالْمَلِكُ قَدْ جَاءَ فِي عَسْكَرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu illā wa-al-maliku qad jāʾa fī ʿaskarihi
sentences.l: And the sun had not risen but the king had already come with his army.
sentences.i: And the sun had scarcely risen when the king was already there with his army.
sentences.n: مَا … إِلَّا وَ is an idiom of immediacy, 'no sooner had X happened than Y' — literally 'X did not happen except that Y [was already the case].'

sentences.t: فَتَدَخَّلَ هُوَ وَأَكَابِرُ دَوْلَتِهِ وَأَمَرَ بَقِيَّةَ عَسْكَرِهِ بِالْوُقُوفِ
sentences.tr: fa-tadakhkhala huwa wa-akābiru dawlatihi wa-amara baqiyyata ʿaskarihi bi-al-wuqūfi
sentences.l: So he entered, he and the great ones of his state, and he commanded the rest of his army to halt.
sentences.i: So he himself went in, together with the great men of his court, and ordered the rest of his army to remain where they stood.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلَ الْمَلِكُ عَلَى الْمَحْسُودِ رَحَّبَ بِهِ وَقَرَّبَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhala al-maliku ʿalā al-maḥsūdi raḥḥaba bihi wa-qarrabahu
sentences.l: So when the king came in to the envied man, he welcomed him, and drew him near.
sentences.i: So when the king came before the envied man, he welcomed him warmly and drew him close.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ أَكَاشِفُكَ عَلَى مَا جِئْتَنَهُ بِهِ قَالَ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu akāshifuka ʿalā mā jiʾtanahu bihi qāla naʿam
sentences.l: And he said to him, 'Shall I lay bare to you what you have come here about?' He said, 'Yes.'
sentences.i: And he said to him, 'Shall I tell you plainly what you have come for?' He said, 'Yes.'
sentences.n: جِئْتَنَهُ به fuses جِئْتَ, 'you came,' with an epenthetic نَ before the enclitic pronoun هُ — a colloquial Egyptian feature (compare forms like قالنله for قال له still heard in speech), standing in for Classical جِئْتَ لَهُ بِهِ, 'you came for it'; kept as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَ إِنَّكَ جِئْتَ تَزُورُنِي وَفِي نَفْسِكَ تَسْئَلُنِي عَنِ ابْنَتِكَ
sentences.tr: qāla innaka jiʾta tazūrunī wa-fī nafsika tasʾalunī ʿani ibnatika
sentences.l: He said, 'Indeed you have come to visit me, and in your inmost self you mean to ask me about your daughter.'
sentences.i: He said, 'You have come to visit me, but in your heart you mean to ask me about your daughter.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ نَعَمْ أَيُّهَا الشَّيْخُ الصَّالِحُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku naʿam ayyuhā al-shaykhu al-ṣāliḥu
sentences.l: Then the king said, 'Yes, O righteous shaykh.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَحْسُودُ أَرْسِلْ مَنْ يَأْتِي بِهَا وَأَرْجُو إِنْشَاءَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى تَبْرَأُ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maḥsūdu arsil man yaʾtī bihā wa-arjū inshāʾa Allāhi taʿālā tabraʾu fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: So the envied man said, 'Send someone who will bring her, and I hope — if God, Most High, wills — she will be cured within this very hour.'
sentences.i: Then the envied man said, 'Send someone to fetch her, and I hope, God willing, that she will be cured this very hour.'
sentences.n: إِنْشَاءَ اللَّهِ fuses إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ, 'if God wills,' into one printed word with no space, as elsewhere in this text; kept as printed and read with its ordinary sense, 'God willing.'

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ الْمَلِكُ وَ أَرْسَلَ خَلْفَ ابْنَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-maliku wa-arsala khalfa ibnatihi
sentences.l: So the king rejoiced, and sent after his daughter.
sentences.i: The king was overjoyed, and sent for his daughter.

sentences.t: وَجَاءُوا بِهَا وَهِيَ مُكَتَّفَةٌ مُغَلَّلَةٌ فَأَجْلَسَهَا الْمَحْسُودُ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾū bihā wa-hiya mukattafatun mughallalatun fa-ajlasahā al-maḥsūdu
sentences.l: And they brought her, she being bound and fettered, and the envied man seated her.
sentences.i: And they brought her in, bound and fettered, and the envied man had her seated [beside him].
sentences.n: مُكَتَّفَةٌ مُغَلَّلَةٌ, 'bound … fettered,' describes her hands tied behind her (كَتَّفَ) and chained (غَلَّلَ) — standard restraints for one thought dangerously possessed.

sentences.t: وَسَتَرَ عَلَيْهَا سِتْرًا وَأَخْرَجَ الشَّعَرَ وَبَخَّرَهَا بِهِ فَصَاحَ الَّذِي كَانَ عَلَى رَاسِهَا وَمَضَى عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-satara ʿalayhā sitran wa-akhraja al-shaʿara wa-bakhkharahā bihi fa-ṣāḥa alladhī kāna ʿalā rāsihā wa-maḍā ʿanhā
sentences.l: And he covered her with a covering, and took out the hair, and fumigated her with it; so the one that was upon her head cried out, and departed from her.
sentences.i: He veiled her, took out the hair, and fumigated her with it — and the thing that had perched on her head cried out and left her.
sentences.n: رَاسِهَا is this text's colloquial spelling of Classical رَأْسِهَا, the hamza consonant simply not pronounced or printed (cf. رَاسَكَ elsewhere in this tale-cycle). الَّذِي كَانَ عَلَى رَاسِهَا, 'the one that was upon her head,' refers to the possessing jinn described earlier as sitting on the possessed girl's head; الشَّعَر is the black cat's hairs the hermit had overheard the jinn name as the cure.

sentences.t: وَعَقَلَتِ الْبِنْتُ عَلَى نَفْسِهَا وَسَتَرَتْ وَجْهَهَا فَقَالَتْ مَا هٰذِهِ الْأَحْوَالُ وَمَنْ جَاءَبِي إِلَى هٰذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿaqalati al-bintu ʿalā nafsihā wa-satarat wajhahā fa-qālat mā hādhihi al-aḥwālu wa-man jāʾa bī ilā hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: And the girl mastered herself, and covered her face, and said: 'What are these conditions? And who brought me to this place?'
sentences.i: The girl came to herself, covered her face, and said, 'What is all this? And who has brought me to this place?'
sentences.n: عَقَلَتْ عَلَى نَفْسِهَا, literally 'she exercised control over herself,' is an idiom built on عَقْل, 'reason' — 'she came to her senses, regained her composure.' جَاءَ بِي, 'he brought me,' uses جَاءَ بِـ exactly as أَتَى بِـ is used below: the verb chooses بِـ for the thing or person brought.

sentences.t: وَفَرِحَ السُّلْطَانُ فَرَحًا مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ وَقَبَّلَ عَيْنَيْهَا وَقَبَّلَ يَدَيِ الشَّيْخِ الْمَحْسُودِ
sentences.tr: wa-fariḥa al-sulṭānu faraḥan mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin wa-qabbala ʿaynayhā wa-qabbala yaday al-shaykhi al-Maḥsūdi
sentences.l: And the sultan rejoiced with a joy beyond which there was no more; and he kissed her eyes, and kissed the hands of the shaykh, al-Maḥsūd.
sentences.i: The sultan rejoiced beyond all measure, and kissed her eyes, and kissed the hands of the shaykh, al-Maḥsūd.
sentences.n: مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ, literally 'there is not, upon it, any increase,' is a fixed idiom of superlative degree — 'to the utmost,' recurring below of the qalandar's own weeping. الْمَحْسُود, 'the Envied One,' and, further on, الْحَاسِد, 'the Envier,' are used throughout as the two men's standing epithets rather than proper names — the hero and his persecutor from the story the qalandar has been telling the efrit.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى أَكَابِرِ دَوْلَتِهِ وَقَٰلَ مَا ذَا نَقُولُونَ مَا يَسْتَأْهِلُ مَنْ شَفَا اِبْنَتِي
sentences.tr: thumma innahu iltafata ilā akābiri dawlatihi wa-qāla mādhā naqūlūna mā yastāhilu man shafā ibnatī
sentences.l: Then indeed he turned to the great ones of his realm, and said: 'What shall we say — what does he who healed my daughter deserve?'
sentences.i: Then he turned to the great men of his realm and said, 'What are we to say — what does the man who cured my daughter deserve?'
sentences.n: نَقُولُونَ carries a non-Classical -ūna ending on a first-person-plural verb (Classical would give نَقُول); kept as printed rather than corrected. يَسْتَاْهِل is colloquial (Egyptian-type) for Classical يَسْتَحِقّ, 'to deserve' — the same everyday word survives in spoken Arabic today.

sentences.t: قَالُوا يَتَزَوَّجُ بِهَا قَٰلَ صَدَقْتُمْ ثُمَّ زَوَّجَهُ بِهَا وَصَارَ الْمَحْسُودُ صِهْرَ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: qālū yatazawwaju bihā qāla ṣadaqtum thumma zawwajahu bihā wa-ṣāra al-Maḥsūdu ṣihra al-maliki
sentences.l: They said: 'Let him marry her.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he married him to her, and al-Maḥsūd became the king's son-in-law.
sentences.n: تَزَوَّجَ بِـ, 'to marry (a woman),' is a form V verb governing بِـ for the woman married — here an optative, 'let him marry her.' زَوَّجَهُ بِهَا, 'he married him to her,' is the causative form II counterpart, governing بِـ the same way.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ مَاتَ الْوَزِيرُ فَقَالَ مَنْ نَعْمَلُ وَزِيرًا فَقَالُوا صِهْرَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda qalīlin māta al-wazīru fa-qāla man naʿmalu wazīran fa-qālū ṣihraka
sentences.l: And after a little, the vizier died; so he said: 'Whom shall we make vizier?' And they said: 'Your son-in-law.'
sentences.i: A little while later the vizier died, and he said, 'Whom shall we make vizier?' They said, 'Your son-in-law.'

sentences.t: فَعَمِلُوا الْمَحْسُودَ وَزِيرًا وَبَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ مَاتَ السُّطَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿamilū al-Maḥsūda wazīran wa-baʿda qalīlin māta al-suṭānu
sentences.l: So they made al-Maḥsūd vizier; and after a little, the sultan died.
sentences.i: So they made al-Maḥsūd vizier; and a little while later the sultan died.
sentences.n: السُّطَان prints without its lām — a compositor's slip for السُّلْطَان, 'the sultan'; the missing letter is not restored, only the printed letters are pointed.

sentences.t: قَالُوا مَنْ نَعْمَلُ مَلِكًا قَالُوا الْوَزِيرَ فَعَمِلُوا الْوَزِيرَ سُلْطَانًا وَصَارَ مَلِكًا حَاكِمًا
sentences.tr: qālū man naʿmalu malikan qālū al-wazīra fa-ʿamilū al-wazīra sulṭānan wa-ṣāra malikan ḥākiman
sentences.l: They said: 'Whom shall we make king?' They said: 'The vizier.' So they made the vizier sultan, and he became king, ruling.
sentences.i: They said, 'Whom shall we make king?' They said, 'The vizier.' So they made the vizier sultan, and he became a reigning king.

sentences.t: فَفِي يَوْمٍ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ رَكِبَ مَرْكَبَهُ وَكَانَ الْحَاسِدُ مَارًّا فِي طَرِيقِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-fī yawmin mina al-ayyāmi rakiba markabahu wa-kāna al-Ḥāsidu mārran fī ṭarīqihi
sentences.l: Then on one of the days, he rode his mount; and al-Ḥāsid happened to be passing along his way,
sentences.i: Then one day, as he rode out, al-Ḥāsid happened to be passing along his way,
sentences.n: مَرْكَب here is his mount for a state procession, not a ship, as it is elsewhere in this same tale.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْمَحْسُودِ بِدَسْتِ مَمْلَكَتِهِ بَيْنَ أُمَرَائِهِ وَوُزَرَائِهِ وَأَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-Maḥsūdi bi-dasti mamlakatihi bayna umarāʾihi wa-wuzarāʾihi wa-arbābi dawlatihi
sentences.l: and behold, there was al-Maḥsūd at the seat of his kingdom, among his emirs, and his viziers, and the lords of his state,
sentences.i: and there, at the seat of his kingdom, was al-Maḥsūd, among his emirs and his viziers and the great men of his state,
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِـ, 'and behold, [there was]...,' is the fixed idhā-of-surprise construction: the بِـ here does not mean 'with' but only marks what suddenly appears (cf. وَإِذَا بِغَزَالَةٍ, 'and behold, a gazelle'). دَسْت is a Persian loanword for a seat or session of state — the royal audience or dais, not a piece of furniture.

sentences.t: فَرَقَعَتْ عَيْنُهُ عَلَى حَاسِدِهِ فَالْتَفَتَ إِلَى بَعْضِ وُزَرَائِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-raqaʿat ʿaynuhu ʿalā ḥāsidihi fa-iltafata ilā baʿḍi wuzarāʾihi
sentences.l: Then his eye fell upon his envier; so he turned to some of his viziers,
sentences.i: Then his eye fell on his envier, and he turned to one of his viziers
sentences.n: رَقَعَتْ is read here by the sense of the standard idiom وَقَعَتْ عَيْنُهُ عَلَى, 'his eye fell upon' — the archive's ر for و may be a compositor's slip, or a genuine variant spelling; the printed letters are kept and pointed as given rather than silently corrected to وَقَعَتْ.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ اِيتِنِي بِذٰلِكَ الرَّجُلِ وَلَا تُرَجِّفْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ītinī bi-dhālika al-rajuli wa-lā turajjifhu
sentences.l: and said: 'Bring me that man, and do not make him afraid.'
sentences.i: and said, 'Bring me that man — but do not frighten him.'
sentences.n: اِيتِنِي spells the imperative of أَتَى بِـ, 'to bring' (literally 'come to me with'), without the hamza a Classical spelling would place on the second letter (اِئْتِنِي); kept as printed. تُرَجِّفْهُ is form II of رَجَفَ, 'to shake, tremble' — causative, 'do not make him tremble,' i.e. 'do not frighten him.'

sentences.t: فَغَابَ وَأَتَاهُ بِالْحَاسِدِ جَارِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ghāba wa-atāhu bi-al-Ḥāsidi jārihi
sentences.l: So he went out of sight, and he brought him al-Ḥāsid, his neighbor,
sentences.i: So the vizier went off, and brought him al-Ḥāsid — his own former neighbor,
sentences.n: أَتَى بِـ, 'to come with,' i.e. 'to bring' — the same verb-plus-preposition idiom as اِيتِنِي بِـ just above. جَارِهِ, 'his neighbor,' quietly identifies al-Ḥāsid as al-Maḥsūd's own former neighbor — the relationship, evidently established earlier in the tale, that first gave rise to the envy.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَعْطُوهُ أَلْفَ مِثْقَالٍ مِنْ خِزَانَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla aʿṭūhu alfa mithqālin min khizānatī
sentences.l: Then he said: 'Give him a thousand mithqāls from my treasury,'
sentences.i: Then he said, 'Give him a thousand gold pieces from my treasury,'
sentences.n: مِثْقَال is a standard unit-weight of gold or silver coin, roughly a dinar's weight — here simply 'a gold piece.'

sentences.t: وَعَبُّوا لَهُ عِشْرِينَ حِمْلًا مِنَ الْمَتْجَرِ وَأَرْسَلُوا مَعَهُ حَارِسًا
sentences.tr: wa-ʿabbū lahu ʿishrīna ḥimlan mina al-matjari wa-arsalū maʿahu ḥārisan
sentences.l: and pack for him twenty loads from the merchandise, and send with him a guard,
sentences.i: and load up twenty pack-loads of goods for him, and send a guard along with him,
sentences.n: عَبَّى, 'to pack, load up,' is a form II verb; الْمَتْجَر, 'merchandise, goods for trade,' is from the same root as تِجَارَة, 'commerce.'

sentences.t: يُوصِلُهُ إِلَى بَلَدِهِ
sentences.tr: yūṣiluhu ilā baladihi
sentences.l: to deliver him to his town.
sentences.i: to see him safely home.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ وَدَّعَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ عَنْهُ وَلَا عَاقَبَهُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu waddaʿahu wa-inṣarafa ʿanhu wa-lā ʿāqabahu ʿalā mā faʿala bihi
sentences.l: Then indeed he bade him farewell, and turned away from him, and did not punish him for what he had done to him.
sentences.i: Then he took leave of him and let him go his way, and did not punish him for what he had done to him.

sentences.t: اُنْظُرْ أَيُّهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ إِلَى عَفْوِ الْمَحْسُودِ إِلَى الْحَاسِدِ
sentences.tr: unẓur ayyuhā al-ʿifrītu ilā ʿafwi al-Maḥsūdi ilā al-Ḥāsidi
sentences.l: Look, O efrit, at the pardon of al-Maḥsūd toward al-Ḥāsid,
sentences.i: See, O efrit, how al-Maḥsūd pardoned al-Ḥāsid,

sentences.t: وَكَيْفَ حَسَدَهُ فِي الْبِدَايَةِ ثُمَّ أَذَاهُ وَسَافَرَ لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-kayfa ḥasadahu fī al-bidāyati thumma adhāhu wa-sāfara lahu
sentences.l: and how he had envied him at the beginning, then harmed him, and journeyed against him,
sentences.i: the man who had envied him from the first, then done him harm, and pursued him from place to place,
sentences.n: أَذَاهُ here is read as a verb, 'he harmed him' — properly آذَاهُ (form IV), the edition's spelling collapsing the initial hamza-plus-alif into a single alif, typical of this Middle Arabic. سَافَرَ لَهُ, literally 'he traveled for him,' is read by sense as 'he journeyed against him, pursued him' — this government of لِـ with سَافَرَ is unusual and its exact force is uncertain.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَلَغَ بِهِ إِلَى أَنْ رَمَى فِي الْبِئْرِ وَ أَرَادَ قَتْلَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma balagha bihi ilā an ramā fī al-biʾri wa-arāda qatlahu
sentences.l: until it brought him to the point that he threw him into the well, and wanted to kill him,
sentences.i: until at last he threw him down into the well, meaning to kill him,
sentences.n: بَلَغَ بِهِ إِلَى أَنْ, literally 'it reached with him to [the point] that,' is an idiom for matters coming to a head — 'things went so far that.'

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يُقَابِلْهُ عَلَى أَذَاهُ بَلْ صَفَحَ عَنْهُ وَعَفَا لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yuqābilhu ʿalā adhāhu bal ṣafaḥa ʿanhu wa-ʿafā lahu
sentences.l: yet he did not repay him for his harm, but rather pardoned him, and forgave him.
sentences.i: yet he did not repay him for the harm he had done, but overlooked it and forgave him outright.
sentences.n: قَابَلَهُ عَلَى, 'to repay/requite him for,' takes عَلَى for the thing repaid. عَفَا لَهُ, 'he forgave him,' uses عَفَا (elsewhere عَفَا عَنْ) with لِـ instead — the لِـ here simply marks the person forgiven, as عَنْهُ does with صَفَحَ just before it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَيْتُ أَيَّتُهَا السَّيِّدَةُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ الْبُكَاءَ الشَّدِيدَ الَّذِي مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ وَ أَنْشَدْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakaytu ayyatuhā al-sayyidatu bayna yadayhi al-bukāʾa al-shadīda alladhī mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin wa-anshadtu
sentences.l: Then I wept, O my lady, before him, weeping so intense there was no more of it; and I recited:
sentences.i: Then, O my lady, I wept before him most bitterly, weeping beyond all measure; and I recited:
sentences.n: أَيَّتُهَا السَّيِّدَةُ marks a brief return of address from the embedded tale — spoken to the efrit — back to the frame in which the qalandar himself is speaking, here to the lady of the house, the same address as يَا سِتِّي elsewhere. الْبُكَاءَ الشَّدِيدَ echoes, as a cognate-style accusative, the same 'beyond which there was no more' idiom used of the sultan's joy above.

sentences.t:
وَهَبَ الْجُنَاةَ فَلَمْ تَزَلْ أَهْلُ النُّهَى * يَهَبُونَ لِلْجَانِينَ مَا يَجْنُونَهُ
فَلَقَدْ حَوَيْتَ عَلَى الذُّنُوبِ بِأَسْرِهَا * فَاحْوِ مِنَ الصَّفْحِ الْجَمِيلِ فُنُونَهُ
فَمَنِ ابْتَغَى عَفْوَ الَّذِي هُوَ فَوْقَهُ * فَلْيَعْفُ عَنْ ذَنْبِ الَّذِي هُوَ دُونَهُ
sentences.tr:
wahaba al-junāta fa-lam tazal ahlu al-nuhā * yahabūna li-al-jānīna mā yajnūnahu
fa-laqad ḥawayta ʿalā al-dhunūbi bi-asrihā * fa-aḥwi mina al-ṣafḥi al-jamīli funūnahu
fa-mani ibtaghā ʿafwa alladhī huwa fawqahu * fa-l-yaʿfu ʿan dhanbi alladhī huwa dūnahu
sentences.l:
He forgave the guilty, for men of understanding never cease * to grant the guilty back the very wrong they did.
For indeed you have taken in every sin in its entirety * so take up, from fair forgiveness, every kind of it.
So whoever seeks the pardon of him who is above him * let him pardon the sin of him who is beneath him.
sentences.i:
He forgave the guilty — for people of true understanding never cease * to grant the guilty pardon for the very wrong they have done.
You have taken in every sin, every one of them — * so take up, from fair forgiveness, every kind there is.
Whoever seeks pardon from one who stands above him * should grant that pardon to one who stands beneath him.
sentences.n: Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be; the pointing is the edition's own. The second line turns to address al-Ḥāsid directly (a shift from third to second person within the same poem): 'you have taken in every sin' concedes that he has committed every kind of wrong, and calls on him to extend as wide a forgiveness as he has just received. الْجُنَاة / يَجْنُونَهُ plays on the single root ج-ن-ي, 'to commit an offense,' across noun and verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ إِمَّا أَنْ أَقْتُلَكَ وَإِمَّا الْعَفْوُ عَنْكَ فَلَا وَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ أَسْحَرَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu immā an aqtulaka wa-immā al-ʿafwu ʿanka fa-lā wa-lā budda an asḥaraka
sentences.l: So the efrit said: 'Either that I kill you, or — as for pardon concerning you — no; and there is no escape but that I enchant you.'
sentences.i: So the efrit said, 'I shall either kill you, or — pardon you? No; but I must at least enchant you.'
sentences.n: لَا بُدَّ أَنْ, literally 'there is no escape that…', is the standard idiom for an unavoidable necessity, 'I must…'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اقْتَلَعَ بِي مِنَ الْأَرْضِ وَطَارَ بِي إِلَى الْجَوِّ حَتَّى نَظَرْتُ إِلَى الدُّنْيَا تَحْتِي كَأَنَّهَا قَصْعَةٌ فِي وَسَطِ الْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: thumma iqtalaʿa bī min al-arḍi wa-ṭāra bī ilā al-jawwi ḥattā naẓartu ilā al-dunyā taḥtī kaʾannahā qaṣʿatun fī wasṭi al-māʾi
sentences.l: Then he plucked me up from the earth, and flew with me into the sky, until I looked down at the world beneath me — as though it were a bowl in the middle of the water.
sentences.i: Then he tore me up from the earth and flew off with me into the sky, until I looked down and saw the whole world beneath me as though it were a single bowl set in the middle of the sea.
sentences.n: قَصْعَةٌ فِي وَسَطِ الْمَاءِ, 'a bowl in the middle of the water,' is the tale's image for how small and enclosed the earth looked from that height — an ordinary bowl set adrift on an expanse of water.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَطَّنِي عَلَى جَبَلٍ وَأَخَذَ قَلِيلًا مِنَ التُّرَابِ وَهَمْهَمَ عَلَيْهِ وَعَزَمَ وَطَرَشَنِي بِهِ وَقَالَ اُخْرُجْ مِنْ هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ إِلَى صُورَةِ قِرْدٍ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaṭṭanī ʿalā jabalin wa-akhadha qalīlan mina al-turābi wa-hamhama ʿalayhi wa-ʿazama wa-ṭarashanī bihi wa-qāla ukhruj min hādhihi al-ṣūrati ilā ṣūrati qirdin
sentences.l: Then he set me down upon a mountain, and took a little of the earth, and murmured over it, and made a conjuration, and flung it at me, and said: 'Get out of this form, into the form of an ape!'
sentences.i: Then he set me down on a mountain, took up a handful of earth, murmured a charm over it, spoke a spell, and flung it at me, saying, 'Out of this shape, and into the shape of an ape!'
sentences.n: هَمْهَمَ, 'murmured' (an onomatopoeic verb), and عَزَمَ, here 'pronounced a binding conjuration' (from عَزِيمَة, an exorcist's spell) rather than its ordinary sense 'resolved,' both describe the efrit's incantation over the earth. طَرَشَنِي بِهِ, literally 'threw at me with it,' uses the colloquial verb طَرَشَ, 'to throw, fling' — not Classical طَرَحَ — with بِهِ marking the handful of earth as the missile, on the pattern of رَمَاهُ بِشَيْءٍ, 'pelted him with something.'

sentences.t: فَمِنْ ذَلِكَ الْوَقْتِ صِرْتُ قِرْدًا ابْنَ مِائَةِ سَنَةٍ فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ نَفْسِي فِي هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ الْقَبِيحَةِ بَكَيْتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي
sentences.tr: fa-min dhālika al-waqti ṣirtu qirdan ibna miʾati sanatin fa-lammā raʾaytu nafsī fī hādhihi al-ṣūrati al-qabīḥati bakaytu ʿalā nafsī
sentences.l: So from that time I became an ape, a hundred years old; and when I saw myself in this ugly form, I wept for myself,
sentences.i: And from that moment I became an ape — a hundred years old, it seemed — and when I saw myself in this hideous shape, I wept for myself,
sentences.n: ابْنَ مِائَةِ سَنَةٍ, literally 'a son of a hundred years,' is the ordinary idiom for stating an age, but its sense here is puzzling, since the qalandar is a young prince newly cursed, not a centenarian. It may be hyperbole for 'an ape through and through,' or mark some unnatural stretch of time worked by the spell; the text does not explain it, and the reading given here simply follows the words as printed.

sentences.t: وَصَبَرْتُ عَلَى جَوْرِ الزَّمَانِ وَعَلِمْتُ أَنَّ الزَّمَانَ لَيْسَ لِأَحَدٍ وَقٰلَ انْحَدَرْتُ مِنْ عَلَى الْجَبَلِ إِلَى أَسْفَلَ فَوَجَدْتُ بَرًّا مُتَّسِعًا فَسَافَرْتُ مُدَّةَ الشَّهْرِ فَانْتَهَى بِي السَّيْرُ إِلَى شَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ الْمَالِحِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣabartu ʿalā jawri al-zamāni wa-ʿalimtu anna al-zamāna laysa li-aḥadin wa-qāla inḥadartu min ʿalā al-jabali ilā asfala fa-wajadtu barran muttasiʿan fa-sāfartu muddata al-shahri fa-intahā bī al-sayru ilā shāṭiʾi al-baḥri al-māliḥi
sentences.l: And I bore patiently the tyranny of time, and knew that time belongs to no one. He said: 'I descended from off the mountain, downward, and found an open expanse of land, and traveled the space of a month, until the journey brought me to the shore of the salt sea.'
sentences.i: I bore the tyranny of fortune patiently, knowing that fortune stays with no one forever. He continued: 'I made my way down from the mountain, and found a wide stretch of open country, and traveled on for the space of a month, until my wandering brought me to the shore of the salt sea.'
sentences.n: الزَّمَانُ, literally 'time,' here means 'fortune, fate' — لَيْسَ لِأَحَدٍ, 'is not for anyone,' meaning fortune belongs permanently to no one. The archive prints قل for قَالَ, its usual defective spelling with the medial alif dropped; pointed here with the dagger alif. As at قَالَ فَرِحْتُ بِوُصُولِي إِلَيْهَا earlier in this same tale, the word works here as a bare narrative tag ('he said/continued') rather than introducing anyone else's speech. شَاطِئِ, 'shore,' is spelled شاطي in the archive, its hamza's seat printed without dots — restored here as elsewhere in this slice (cf. مِائَةِ above).

sentences.t: فَوَقَفْتُ سَاعَةً وَإِذَا أَنَا بِمَرْكَبٍ فِي وَسَطِ الْبَحْرِ وَقَدْ طَابَ رِيحُهُ وَهُوَ طَالِبُ الْبَرِّ
sentences.tr: fa-waqaftu sāʿatan wa-idhā anā bi-markabin fī wasṭi al-baḥri wa-qad ṭāba rīḥuhu wa-huwa ṭālibu al-barri
sentences.l: So I stood a while, and behold, [there was] I with a ship in the middle of the sea, its wind having turned fair, and it heading for the shore.
sentences.i: So I stood there a while, and suddenly I found myself with a ship out in the middle of the sea, its wind blowing fair, making for land.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا أَنَا بِـ, 'and behold, I [was] with…,' is the same إِذَا of surprise met earlier in this text's frame narration, here marking the ship's sudden appearance; the بِـ that follows only marks what appears. طَالِبُ الْبَرِّ, literally 'seeking the shore,' describes the ship as heading toward land.

sentences.t: فَاخْتَفَيْتُ خَلْفَ صَخْرَةٍ عَلَى جَانِبِ الْبَرِّ وَصَبَرْتُ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَى الْمَرْكَبُ فَنَزَلْتُ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ikhtafaytu khalfa ṣakhratin ʿalā jānibi al-barri wa-ṣabartu ilā an atā al-markabu fa-nazaltu fīhi
sentences.l: So I hid myself behind a rock, at the edge of the shore, and I waited until the ship came, and I got down into it.
sentences.i: So I hid behind a rock at the shore's edge, and waited until the ship drew near, then swam out and boarded it.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاحِدٌ مِنَ الرُّكَّابِ أَخْرِجُوا هَذَا الْمَشُومَ عَنَّا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wāḥidun mina al-rukkābi akhrijū hādhā al-mashūma ʿannā
sentences.l: So one of the passengers said: 'Cast this ill-omened creature away from us!'
sentences.i: Then one of the passengers said, 'Throw this ill-omened creature off, away from us!'
sentences.n: الْمَشُوم, 'ill-omened, unlucky,' is this text's colloquial spelling of Classical مَشْؤُوم, dropping its hamza altogether.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الرَّئِسُ نَقْتُلُهُ وَ قَالَ الْآخَرُ اُقْتُلْهُ بِهَذَا السَّيْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-raʾisu naqtuluhu wa qāla al-ākharu uqtulhu bi-hādhā al-sayfi
sentences.l: So the captain said: 'We will kill him'; and the other said: 'Kill him with this sword!'
sentences.i: The captain said, 'Let us kill him'; but the other said, 'Kill him with this sword!'
sentences.n: الرَّئِس, 'the captain, chief,' is this text's short spelling of the fuller رَئِيس, dropping its long ī; kept as printed and read by sense, and it recurs through the rest of the tale for the ship's captain. The archive's line break falls here between نَقْتُلُهُ and قَالَ, printing the وَ alone at the line's edge before rejoining the verb — a recurring artifact of this printing rather than a textual feature; the same thing happens again below, between اسْتَجَارَ بِي and قٰلَ أَجَرْتُهُ.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكْتُ ذَيْلَ الرَّئِسِ وَبَكَيْتُ وَسَالَتْ دُمُوعِي
sentences.tr: fa-masaktu dhayla al-raʾisi wa-bakaytu wa-sālat dumūʿī
sentences.l: So I seized the captain's hem, and wept, and my tears flowed.
sentences.i: So I took hold of the captain's skirts, and wept, my tears streaming.
sentences.n: ذَيْل, 'hem, skirt (of a garment),' — grasping someone's hem is the conventional gesture of pleading for mercy.

sentences.t: فَحَنَّ عَلَى الرَّئِسِ وَقَالَ يَا تُجَّارُ هَذَا الْقِرْدُ قَدِ اسْتَجَارَ بِي وَ قٰلَ أَجَرْتُهُ وَهُوَ فِي ذِمَامِي فَلَا أَحَدَ يُعَكِّرُ عَلَيْهِ وَلَا يُشَوِّشُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥanna ʿalā al-raʾisi wa-qāla yā tujjāru hādhā al-qirdu qadi istajāra bī wa qāla ajartuhu wa-huwa fī dhimāmī fa-lā aḥada yuʿakkiru ʿalayhi wa-lā yushawwishu ʿalayhi
sentences.l: So compassion came over the captain, and he said: 'O merchants, this ape has sought refuge with me.' He said: 'I have granted him my protection, and he is under my safeguard — so let no one trouble him, nor disturb him.'
sentences.i: So the captain was moved to pity, and said, 'O merchants, this ape has thrown himself on my protection.' Then he went on, 'I have granted him refuge — he is under my safeguard, so let no one trouble or disturb him.'
sentences.n: فَحَنَّ عَلَى الرَّئِسِ, literally 'then compassion came upon the captain,' uses عَلَى to mark the person an emotion affects, the same construction as غَارَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَقُّ met earlier in this story. The second قٰلَ is again the defective spelling of قَالَ, here simply re-marking that the captain continues speaking, not introducing a new speaker. ذِمَامِي, 'my dhimām,' is the captain's own personal pledge of safe-conduct — a formal guarantee, binding on everyone aboard, that the one it covers will not be harmed. يُعَكِّرُ عَلَيْهِ and يُشَوِّشُ عَلَيْهِ, 'trouble him' and 'disturb him,' are near-synonyms doubled for emphasis.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الرَّئِسَ صَارَ يُحْسِنُ إِلَيَّ وَمَهْمَا تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ أَفْهَمُهُ وَأَقْضِي حَوَائِجَهُ كُلَّهَا وَأَخْدُمُهُ فِي الْمَرْكَبِ فَحَبَّنِي
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-raʾisa ṣāra yuḥsinu ilayya wa-mahmā takallama bihi afhamuhu wa-aqḍī ḥawāʾijahu kullahā wa-akhdumuhu fī al-markabi fa-ḥabbanī
sentences.l: Then indeed the captain began to be kind to me, and whatever he spoke, I understood it, and I fulfilled all his needs, and I served him aboard the ship — so he grew fond of me.
sentences.i: Then the captain grew kind to me; whatever he said, I understood at once, and I saw to all his needs and served him about the ship, until he became fond of me.
sentences.n: فَحَبَّنِي, 'he grew fond of me,' uses the plain Classical verb حَبَّ, 'to love,' beside the more usual form IV أَحَبَّ — both are attested, but حَبَّ is the rarer of the two in ordinary prose.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَرْكَبَ طَابَ لَهُ الرِّيحُ مُدَّةَ خَمْسِينَ يَوْمًا فَرَسَيْنَا عَلَى مَدِينَةٍ عَظِيمَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-markaba ṭāba lahu al-rīḥu muddata khamsīna yawman fa-rasaynā ʿalā madīnatin ʿaẓīmatin
sentences.l: Then indeed the ship — the wind turned fair for it for the space of fifty days — and we anchored at a great city.
sentences.i: Then the ship had fair sailing winds for fifty days together, until we anchored off a great city.
sentences.n: رَسَيْنَا, 'we anchored,' is this text's spelling of the defective verb رَسَا with its final radical written يَ rather than وَ — the same kind of spelling seen in شَدَّيْنَا and رَدَّيْنَا elsewhere in this story.

sentences.t: وَفِيهَا عَالَمٌ عَظِيمٌ لَا يُحْصَى عَدَدُهُمْ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
sentences.tr: wa-fīhā ʿālamun ʿaẓīmun lā yuḥṣā ʿadaduhum illā Allāhu
sentences.l: and in it were a great multitude of people whose number none could count save God.
sentences.i: and in it were throngs of people beyond counting, save by God alone.
sentences.n: عَالَمٌ عَظِيمٌ, literally 'a great world,' idiomatically means simply 'a vast multitude, throngs of people.'

sentences.t: فَسَاعَةَ وُصُولِنَا وَقَفَ مَرْكَبُنَا وَإِذَا قَدْ جَاءَتْ لَنَا مَمَالِيكُ مِنْ جِهَةِ مَلِكِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-sāʿata wuṣūlinā waqafa markabunā wa-idhā qad jāʾat lanā mamālīku min jihati maliki al-madīnati
sentences.l: So at the moment of our arrival, our ship stopped, and behold, mamluks had already come to us on behalf of the city's king,
sentences.i: The moment we arrived, our ship came to a stop, and there, mamluks had already come out to us on behalf of the city's king,
sentences.n: مَمَالِيك, 'mamluks,' were the king's own retainer-slaves, here sent on a ceremonial errand to welcome arriving merchants.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعُوا إِلَى مَرْكَبِنَا وَهَنَّوْا التُّجَّارَ بِالسَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿū ilā markabinā wa-hannaw al-tujjāra bi-al-salāmati
sentences.l: and they came up to our ship, and congratulated the merchants on their safe arrival,
sentences.i: and they came aboard our ship and wished the merchants joy of their safe arrival,
sentences.n: هَنَّوْا, 'they congratulated,' is spelled هنوا in the archive, dropping the hamza of Classical هَنَّأُوا altogether — the same colloquial simplification as الْمَشُوم above.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا مَلِكُنَا يُهَنِّئُكُمْ بِالسَّلَامَةِ وَقَدْ أَرْسَلَ إِلَيْكُمْ هَذَا الدَّرْجَ الْوَرَقَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū malikunā yuhanniʾukum bi-al-salāmati wa-qad arsala ilaykum hādhā al-darja al-waraqa
sentences.l: and they said: 'Our king wishes you joy of your safety, and he has sent to you this roll of paper,
sentences.i: and said, 'Our king congratulates you on your safe arrival, and he has sent you this roll of paper,
sentences.n: يُهَنِّئُكُم, 'congratulates you,' is spelled يهنيكم in the archive, its hamza's seat printed without dots — restored here as elsewhere in this slice (cf. مِائَةِ, شَاطِئِ above).

sentences.t: وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْكُمْ يَكْتُبُ فِيهِ سَطْرًا وَاحِدًا
sentences.tr: wa-kullu wāḥidin minkum yaktubu fīhi saṭran wāḥidan
sentences.l: and let every one of you write in it one line —
sentences.i: and every one of you is to write a single line on it —

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ الْمَلِكَ كَانَ لَهُ وَزِيرٌ خَطَّاطٌ وَقَدْ مَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-inna al-malika kāna lahu wazīrun khaṭṭāṭun wa-qad māta
sentences.l: for indeed the king had a vizier, a calligrapher, and he had died,
sentences.i: for the king had a vizier, a fine calligrapher, who has now died,

sentences.t: وَأَقْسَمَ السُّلْطَانُ وَحَلَفَ الْأَيْمَانَ الْعِظَامَ بِأَنْ لَا يُوَزَّرَ إِلَّا مَنْ يَكْتُبُ مِثْلَ خَطِّهِ
sentences.tr: wa-aqsama al-sulṭānu wa-ḥalafa al-aymāna al-ʿiẓāma bi-an lā yuwazzara illā man yaktubu mithla khaṭṭihi
sentences.l: and the sultan swore, and swore mighty oaths, that none should be made vizier except one who could write the like of his handwriting.
sentences.i: and the sultan took a solemn vow, swearing mighty oaths, that he would appoint no one vizier save a man who could write as well as his hand.
sentences.n: أَقْسَمَ and حَلَفَ الْأَيْمَانَ, both 'swore, took an oath,' are stacked as a doubled intensifier, in the manner of فُحِّمَ سُوِّدَ elsewhere in this story. يُوَزَّرَ, 'be made vizier,' treats الوزارة as a verb of appointment in the passive.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَاوَلَ التُّجَّارَ دَرْجَ وَرَقٍ طُولُهُ عَشَرَةُ أَذْرُعٍ فِي عَرْضِ ذِرَاعٍ
sentences.tr: thumma nāwala al-tujjāra darja waraqin ṭūluhu ʿasharatu adhruʿin fī ʿarḍi dhirāʿin
sentences.l: Then he handed the merchants a roll of paper whose length was ten cubits, in a width of one cubit.
sentences.i: Then he handed the merchants a roll of paper ten cubits long by one cubit wide.

sentences.t: فَكَتَبَ كُلُّ مَنْ كَانَ يَعْرِفُ الْكِتَابَةَ إِلَى آخِرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-kataba kullu man kāna yaʿrifu al-kitābata ilā ākhirihim
sentences.l: So everyone who knew how to write, wrote — down to the last of them.
sentences.i: So every man who knew how to write wrote his line, down to the very last of them,

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ وَأَنَا فِي صُورَةِ الْقِرْدِ وَخَطَفْتُ الدَّرْجَ مِنْ أَيْدِيهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu wa-anā fī ṣūrati al-qirdi wa-khaṭaftu al-darja min aydīhim
sentences.l: So I rose — I, in the shape of the ape — and I snatched the roll from their hands,
sentences.i: So I got up, ape though I seemed, and snatched the scroll from their hands,

sentences.t: فَخَافُوا أَنِّي أَقْطَعُهُ فَنَهَرُونِي
sentences.tr: fa-khāfū annī aqṭaʿuhu fa-naharūnī
sentences.l: So they feared that I would tear it, and they rebuked me sharply.
sentences.i: for they feared I meant to tear it up, and drove me off with sharp words.
sentences.n: نَهَرُونِي, 'they rebuked/scolded me sharply,' closes the slice on their alarm at the ape's boldness — taken up again as the next scene opens.

sentences.t: فَأَشَرْتُ إِلَيْهِمْ أَنِّي أَكْتُبُ فَأَشَارَ لَهُمُ الرَّئِيسُ خَلْوَةً؛
sentences.tr: fa-ashartu ilayhim annī aktubu fa-ashāra lahumu al-raʾīsu khalwatan;
sentences.l: So I gestured to them that I write; so the captain gestured to them, privately.
sentences.i: So I made a sign to them that I only meant to write; and the captain drew the rest aside and signaled to them, privately.
sentences.n: خَلْوَةً is read as an adverbial accusative ('privately, apart'), describing how the captain signaled the rest of the crew — not as an imperative 'leave him' (خَلُّوهُ), which the archive's own letters (خ-ل-و-ة) do not spell.

sentences.t: طَرَدْنَا عَنَّا وَإِنْ أَحْسَنَ الْكِتابَةَ اِتَّخَذْنٰهُ وَإِلَّا فَإِنِّي بِنَهْ ثُمَّ إِنِّي مَسَكْتُ الْقَلَمَ وَاِسْتَعْمَلِيتُ مِنْ الدَّوَاةِ الرُّقَاعِيَّ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ ش —
sentences.tr: ṭaradnā ʿannā wa-in aḥsana al-kitābata ittakhadhnāhu wa-illā fa-innī binah thumma innī masaktu al-qalama wa-istaʿmalītu min al-dawāti al-ruqāʿiyya hadhayni al-baytayni sh —
sentences.l: We would drive [him] away from us — but if he did well at the writing, we would take him; and if not, then indeed I would be rid of him. Then I took up the pen, and used, from the inkstand, the Ruqʿa one; these two verses — verse:
sentences.i: We meant to put him off the ship — but if he wrote well, we would keep him, and if not, we would be rid of him. Then I took up the pen, dipped it from the inkstand in the Ruqʿa hand, and wrote these two lines, in verse:
sentences.n: اِتَّخَذْنٰهُ is printed اتخذنه, missing the long ا before the object suffix ـه; the missing vowel is pointed here with the dagger alif (ـٰ) rather than the spelling rewritten. بِنَهْ, after وَإِلَّا فَإِنِّي, is textually obscure: the sense wanted is some fate for the ape if his writing failed, but the letters do not parse as a standard word and may be a compositor's slip; kept and vocalized only minimally. وَاسْتَعْمَلِيتُ spells the 1st-person ending with an extra ي (istaʿmalītu for istaʿmaltu), a colloquial spelling this edition uses elsewhere for this same ending. الرُّقَاعِيَّ, 'the Ruqʿa one', is read as an accusative adjective describing 'the pen' named a few words earlier, despite the intervening clause — an awkward word order kept as printed. ش abbreviates شِعْر ('poetry'), the rubric this passage prints before each of its five quoted verses; it and the dash that follows are the edition's own convention, not part of any poem.

sentences.t:
لَقَدْ كَتَبَ الدَّهْرُ فَضْلَ الْكِرَامِ * وَفَضْلُكَ لِلْآنِ
فَلَا اَيْتَمَ اللهُ مِنْكَ الْوَرَى * لَاَنَّكَ لِلْاَفْضَلِ
sentences.tr:
laqad kataba al-dahru faḍla al-kirāmi * wa-faḍluka li-al-āni
fa-lā aytama Allāhu minka al-warā * la-annaka li-al-afḍali
sentences.l:
Time has indeed recorded the excellence of the noble ones, * and your excellence belongs to now, too.
So may God not bereave mankind of you, * for indeed you are for the most excellent.
sentences.i: Time has set down the excellence of the noble, and your own excellence is written for this very hour. So may God never take you from mankind, for truly you are among the very best.
sentences.n: أَيْتَمَ (form IV of يتم, 'to orphan, bereave') is printed اَيْتَمَ, its hamza left entirely unmarked even though the vowel is pointed; kept exactly as the archive gives it, per the rule of copying pointed verse-words unchanged. لَاَنَّكَ, likewise printed without a hamza mark, is read as لَأَنَّكَ — the emphatic lām + أَنَّ ('for indeed you...'), not the causal لِأَنَّ ('because'). لِلْآنِ, 'to the present now', opens the theme this whole florilegium returns to: time preserves the excellence of a fine hand into the present.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبْتُ بِقَلَمِ الرَّيْحَانِ ش —
sentences.tr: wa-katabtu bi-qalami al-rayḥāni sh —
sentences.l: And I wrote, in the pen of Rayḥān — verse:
sentences.i: And I wrote in the Rayḥānī hand — in verse:
sentences.n: الرَّيْحَان ('basil'), one of the classical Arabic calligraphic hands, a rounded cursive script; ش again abbreviates شِعْر.

sentences.t:
لَهُ قَلَمٌ عَمَّ الْاَقَالِيمَ نَفْعُهُ * وَعَمَّ جَمِيعِ
فَمَا نِيلُ مِصْرَ مِثْلَ نَائِلِكَ الَّذِي * يَمِيلُ اِلَى الْاَمْصَارِ
sentences.tr:
lahu qalamun ʿamma al-aqālīma nafʿuhu * wa-ʿamma jamīʿi
fa-mā nīlu miṣra mithla nāʾilika alladhī * yamīlu ilā al-amṣāri
sentences.l:
He has a pen whose benefit has encompassed the climes, * and encompassed the whole of…
For the Nile of Egypt is not like your bounty, which * inclines toward the lands.
sentences.i: He has a pen whose benefit has spread over every clime, and over the whole of… For the Nile of Egypt is nothing beside your bounty, which flows out to every land.
sentences.n: The first line's second hemistich breaks off after جَمِيعِ ('the whole of...'); the print gives no more, as with several other lines in this florilegium. نَائِلِكَ ('your gift, your bounty') puns on نِيل ('the Nile'), the couplet's central conceit: the pen's generosity said to outdo even Egypt's river.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبْتُ بِقَلَمِ الثُّلُثِ ش —
sentences.tr: wa-katabtu bi-qalami al-thuluthi sh —
sentences.l: And I wrote, in the pen of the Third — verse:
sentences.i: And I wrote in the Thuluth hand — in verse:
sentences.n: الثُّلُث ('the third'), an ornamental script named for the proportion of its straight strokes to its curves.

sentences.t:
وَمَا مِنْ كَاتِبٍ اِلَّا سَيَفْنَى * وَيَبْقَى الدَّهْرَ مَا
فَلَا تَكْتُبْ بِكَفِّكَ غَيْرَ شَيْءٍ * يَسُرُّكَ فِي الْقِيَامَةِ
sentences.tr:
wa-mā min kātibin illā sa-yafnā * wa-yabqā al-dahra mā
fa-lā taktub bi-kaffika ghayra shayʾin * yasurruka fī al-qiyāmati
sentences.l:
There is no writer but he shall perish, * and there remains, for all of time, what…
So write not, with your own hand, anything * but what will please you on the Day of Resurrection.
sentences.i: No writer lives but he must perish — yet what remains, for all of time, is what… So write with your own hand nothing but what will gladden you on the Day of Resurrection.
sentences.n: The first line's second hemistich breaks off after مَا ('what...'); the print does not complete it. The couplet's commonplace — every scribe must die, but what his pen once set down outlives him, so write only what will please you at the Resurrection — recurs across Arabic gnomic verse on writing, and echoes this florilegium's own opening claim that time itself records the excellence of the noble.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبْتُ بِقَلَمِ النَّسْخِ ش—
sentences.tr: wa-katabtu bi-qalami al-naskhi sh—
sentences.l: And I wrote, in the pen of Copying — verse:
sentences.i: And I wrote in the Naskh hand — in verse:
sentences.n: النَّسْخ ('copying'), the everyday book-hand from which today's printed Arabic type descends.

sentences.t:
وَلَمَّا نَبَيْنَا بِالْفِرَاقِ * وَحَكَمَتْ فِينَا بِذَاكَ
غَلَوْنَا لِاَفْوَاهِ الْمَحَابِرِ تَشْتَكِي * اَلَمَ الْفِرَاقِ بَا
sentences.tr:
wa-lammā nabaynā bi-al-firāqi * wa-ḥakamat fīnā bidhāka
ghalawnā li-afwāhi al-maḥābiri tashtakī * alama al-firāqi bā
sentences.l:
And when we were estranged through parting, * and it had judged against us by that,
we bent low to the mouths of the inkstands, complaining * of the pain of parting…
sentences.i: And when we were sundered by parting, and fate had decreed it so for us, we bowed to the very mouths of the inkwells, which complain of the pain of parting…
sentences.n: نَبَيْنَا is printed exactly so, its hamza unmarked; it is read here as expressing estrangement (compare نَأَيْنَا, 'we grew distant'), though the form is obscure and may be a copying error. الْمَحَابِرِ ('the inkstands') تَشْتَكِي, 'complain' — pen and inkwell personified as grieving their user's parting, the same conceit that runs through this whole florilegium. The second line's second hemistich breaks off mid-word after بَا; the print gives no more.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبْتُ بِقَلَمِ الطُّومَهِ —
sentences.tr: wa-katabtu bi-qalami al-ṭūmahi —
sentences.l: And I wrote, in the pen of the Ṭūmah —
sentences.i: And I wrote in the Ṭūmār hand —
sentences.n: الطُّومَه is this text's clipped spelling of الطُّومار (ṭūmār), the grand chancery hand used for state proclamations and caliphal decrees — fittingly, for the verse that follows concerns the caliphate. Unlike the four tags before it, the archive omits the ش (شِعْر) rubric here before the dash; kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ الْخِلَافَةَ لَا تَدُومُ لِوَاحِدٍ * اِنْ كُنْتَ تُنكِرُ
وَاكْتُبْ بِخَيْرٍ اِذَا مَاكُنْتَ مُقْتَدِرًا * فَقُلْ نُسِبَتْ بِهَذَا النَسَبِ وَالْقَلَمِ
sentences.tr:
inna al-khilāfata lā tadūmu li-wāḥidin * in kunta tunkiru
wa-uktub bi-khayrin idhā mā kunta muqtadiran * fa-qul nusibat bi-hādhā al-nasabi wa-al-qalami
sentences.l:
Indeed, the caliphate does not last for any one man, * if you should deny it…
and write with good, whenever you are able, * then say: 'It was ascribed, by this lineage and the pen.'
sentences.i: The caliphate endures for no one man forever — deny it if you will… So write well while you still hold the power to, and you may say: 'It was this pen, and this pedigree, that earned it.'
sentences.n: The first line's second hemistich breaks off after تُنكِرُ ('you deny'), with no object given. نُسِبَتْ ('it was ascribed'), feminine, most likely refers back to الْخِلَافَةَ: succession is legitimated — 'ascribed' — by lineage and by the pen that records it, closing the florilegium on the same note it opened with, that the pen outlasts, and vindicates, its holder.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَاوَلْتُهُمُ الدَّرْجَ وَكَتَبُوا كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ سَطْرًا
sentences.tr: thumma nāwaltuhumu al-darja wa-katabū kullu wāḥidin saṭran
sentences.l: Then I handed them the scroll, and they wrote — each one — a line,
sentences.i: Then I handed them the scroll, and each of them wrote a line,

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذُوهُ وَطَلَعُوا بِهِ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhūhu wa-ṭalaʿū bihi ilā al-maliki
sentences.l: then they took it, and went up with it to the king.
sentences.i: then they took it and went up with it to the king.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى الدَّرْجِ فَلَمْ يُعْجِبْهُ خَطُّ أَحَدٍ إِلَّا خَطِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẕara al-maliku ilā al-darji fa-lam yuʿjibhu khaṭṭu aḥadin illā khaṭṭī
sentences.l: And when the king looked at the scroll, no one's hand pleased him except my hand.
sentences.i: And when the king looked over the scroll, no one's handwriting pleased him but mine.
sentences.n: فَلَمَّا … فَلَمْ doubles the resumptive فَـ, once after لَمَّا and once before the main verb — a recurring pattern in this narrator's prose (Classical usage would generally drop the second one).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِلْجَمَاعَةِ تَوَجَّهُوا إِلَى صَاحِبِ هَذَا الْخَطِّ وَأَرْكِبُوهُ بَغْلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-al-jamāʿati tawajjahū ilā ṣāḥibi hādhā al-khaṭṭi wa-arkibūhu baghlatan
sentences.l: So he said to the company: 'Go to the owner of this hand, and mount him upon a mule,

sentences.t: وَهَاتُوهُ بِالنَّوْبَةِ وَأَلْبِسُوهُ بَدْلَةً سَنِيَّةً وَأَحْضِرُوهُ إِلَى عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: wa-hātūhu bi-al-nawbati wa-albisūhu badlatan saniyyatan wa-aḥḍirūhu ilā ʿindī
sentences.l: and bring him with the band, and clothe him in a splendid robe, and bring him to my presence.'
sentences.i: and bring him with a musical escort, clothe him in a robe of splendor, and bring him before me.'
sentences.n: النَّوْبَة, 'turn, shift,' also names a ceremonial band that plays at set hours — hence 'musical escort' here. هَاتُوا is the colloquial imperative of أَتَى, 'bring,' beside literary اِيتُوا/أَحْضِرُوا.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا كَلَامَ الْمَلِكِ تَبَسَّمُوا فَغَضِبَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū kalāma al-maliki tabassamū fa-ghaḍiba al-maliku minhum
sentences.l: And when they heard the king's words, they smiled; so the king grew angry at them,
sentences.i: And when they heard the king's words, they smiled; and the king grew angry with them,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا مَلَاعِينُ أَقُولُ لَكُمْ عَلَى أَمْرٍ تَضْحَكُونَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā malāʿīnu aqūlu lakum ʿalā amrin taḍḥakūna ʿalayya
sentences.l: and said: 'O accursed ones, I speak to you of a matter, and you laugh at me?'
sentences.i: and said: 'You wretches — I tell you a matter, and you laugh at me?'
sentences.n: The clause carries no interrogative particle; tone alone marks the rhetorical question, as elsewhere in this narrative style.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنَّ لِضَحْكِنَا سَبَبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālū ayyuhā al-maliku inna li-ḍaḥkinā sababan
sentences.l: So they said: 'O King, indeed our laughter has a cause.'
sentences.i: They said: 'O King, our laughter has a reason.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَمَا هُوَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-mā huwa
sentences.l: So he said: 'And what is it?'
sentences.i: 'And what is that?' he asked.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ أَنْتَ تَأْمُرُنَا أَنَّنَا نُحْضِرَ لَكَ الَّذِي كَتَبَ هَذَا الْخَطَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū ayyuhā al-maliku anta taʾmurunā annanā nuḥḍira laka alladhī kataba hādhā al-khaṭṭa
sentences.l: So they said: 'O King, you command us that we bring to you the one who wrote this hand —
sentences.i: They said: 'O King, you command us to bring you the one who wrote this hand —

sentences.t: وَ الْحَالُ أَنَّ الَّذِي كَتَبَهُ قِرْدٌ وَلَيْسَ هُوَ آدَمِيٌّ وَهُوَ مَعَ رَئْسِ الْمَرْكَبِ
sentences.tr: wa al-ḥālu anna alladhī katabahu qirdun wa-laysa huwa ādamiyyun wa-huwa maʿa raʾsi al-markabi
sentences.l: and the fact is that the one who wrote it is an ape, and he is not a human being, and he is with the captain of the ship.'
sentences.i: when the truth is that the one who wrote it is an ape, not a human being at all, and he is with the ship's captain.'
sentences.n: The archive prints a bare وَ alone at this line's edge (P95L08) before الحال begins the next line (P95L09); that split is kept exactly as printed, giving an isolated وَ before its word, rather than silently rejoined. آدَمِيٌّ is pointed as printed, as though nominative, rather than with the extra الف Classical orthography would need for the accusative predicate of لَيْسَ (آدَمِيًّا) — the edition's rasm (four letters, no final alif) cannot support that extra letter, so the case is read as the rasm allows, the same loose pattern as مَلِكٌ for the accusative predicate of كَانَ elsewhere in this story. رَئْس (also below) spells 'captain, ship's-master' without the internal يَاء that Classical رَئِيس would have — a colloquial contraction (roughly 'reʾs'), kept as printed and pointed accordingly throughout this slice.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَ حَقًّا مَا تَقُولُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla a-ḥaqqan mā taqūlūna
sentences.l: So he said: 'Is it, truly, what you are saying?'
sentences.i: So he said: 'Is it true, what you're saying?'
sentences.n: The interrogative hamza أَ is printed as its own detached letter in the archive (P95L10), kept here as its own token rather than joined to حَقًّا.

sentences.t: قَالُوا أَيْوَا وَحَقِّ نِعْمَتِكَ
sentences.tr: qālū aywā wa-ḥaqqi niʿmatika
sentences.l: They said: 'Yes indeed! And by the right of your bounty —
sentences.i: They said: 'Yes indeed, by the truth of your grace —
sentences.n: أَيْوَا is colloquial Egyptian Arabic for 'yes,' not Classical نَعَمْ — a direct intrusion of the vernacular, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْ كَلَامِهِمْ وَاهْتَزَّ مِنَ الطَّرَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-maliku min kalāmihim wa-ihtazza mina al-ṭarabi
sentences.l: so the king marveled at their words, and quivered from delight,
sentences.i: the king marveled at their words, and thrilled with delight,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشْتَرِيَ هَذَا الْقِرْدَ مِنَ الرَّئْسِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla urīdu an ashtariya hādhā al-qirda mina al-raʾsi
sentences.l: and said: 'I want to buy this ape from the captain.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعَثَ رَسُولًا إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَمَعَهُ الْبَغْلَةُ وَالْبَدْلَةُ وَالنَّوْبَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿatha rasūlan ilā al-markabi wa-maʿahu al-baghlatu wa-al-badlatu wa-al-nawbatu
sentences.l: Then he sent a messenger to the ship, with him the mule, and the robe, and the band,
sentences.i: Then he sent a messenger to the ship, bringing with him the mule, the robe, and the musical escort,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَابُدَّ أَنْ تُلْبِسُوهُ هَذِهِ الْبَدْلَةَ وَتُرْكِبُوهُ الْبَغْلَةَ وَتَجِيئُو بِهِ فِي الْمَرْكَبِ وَتَأْتُوا بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lā budda an tulbisūhu hādhihi al-badlata wa-turkibūhu al-baghlata wa-tajīʾū bihi fī al-markabi wa-taʾtū bihi
sentences.l: and said: 'You must clothe him in this robe, and mount him on the mule, and bring him in the ship, and bring him.'
sentences.i: and said: 'You must dress him in this robe, mount him on the mule, bring him aboard the ship, and bring him here.'
sentences.n: تَجِيئُو … وَتَأْتُوا بِهِ pairs two near-synonymous verbs of coming/bringing back to back, likely an intensifying doublet. تَجِيئُو is printed without the final الف that Classical spelling of the same subjunctive تَجِيئُوا would carry — a bare orthographic variant with no difference in sound, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَسَارُوا إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَأَخَذُونِي مِنَ الرَّئْسِ
sentences.tr: fa-sārū ilā al-markabi wa-akhadhūnī mina al-raʾsi
sentences.l: So they went to the ship, and took me from the captain,
sentences.i: So they went to the ship and took me from the captain,

sentences.t: وَ أَلْبَسُونِي الْبَدْلَةَ وَأَرْكَبُونِي الْبَغْلَةَ
sentences.tr: wa albasūnī al-badlata wa-arkabūnī al-baghlata
sentences.l: and clothed me in the robe, and mounted me on the mule,
sentences.i: dressed me in the robe, and set me on the mule,
sentences.n: Another bare وَ stands alone at this line's edge (P95L14) before أَلْبَسُونِي begins the next line (P95L15); kept exactly as printed, as above.

sentences.t: فَانْدَهَشَ الْخَلَائِقُ وَانْقَلَبَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ لِأَجْلِي وَصَارُوا يَتَفَرَّجُونَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-indahasha al-khalāʾiqu wa-inqalabati al-madīnatu li-ajlī wa-ṣārū yatafarrajūna ʿalayya
sentences.l: and the creatures were astonished, and the city was overturned on account of me, and they fell to gazing at me,
sentences.i: the people were astonished, the whole city was thrown into an uproar over me, and everyone fell to staring at me,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا طَلَعُوا بِي إِلَى الْمَلِكِ ر لَاقَانِي قَبَّلْتُ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ ثَلٰثَ مَرَّاتٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṭalaʿū bī ilā al-maliki r lāqānī qabbaltu al-arḍa bayna yadayhi thalātha marrātin
sentences.l: And when they brought me up to the king — r — he met me; I kissed the ground before him three times,
sentences.i: And when they brought me before the king, he received me, and I kissed the ground before him three times,
sentences.n: A single letter ر stands between الملك and لاقاني in the archive (P95L16), unexplained — an isolated fragment, possibly a stray remnant of a longer word (compare this edition's other compositor's slips); it is kept as printed and left untranslated. لَاقَانِي (form III of لَقِيَ, 'meet, encounter') is read as the king's own action, 'he received/met me.' ثَلٰث spells 'three' without the internal الف Classical ثَلَاث would carry — pointed here with the dagger alif (ـٰ) as this edition's defective spellings are throughout, preserving the rasm while reading correctly.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَنِي بِالْجُلُوسِ فَجَلَسْتُ عَلَى رُكْبَتَيَّ
sentences.tr: thumma amaranī bi-al-julūsi fa-jalastu ʿalā rukbatayya
sentences.l: then he ordered me to sit, so I sat upon my two knees,
sentences.i: then he bade me sit, so I knelt down,
sentences.n: بِالْجُلُوسِ: بِـ marks the content of the command after أَمَرَ بِـ, 'commanded [him] to' — the verb's regular preposition (cf. بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ).

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَتِ الْخَلَائِقُ الْحَاضِرِينَ مِنْ أَدَبِي وَكَانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ تَعَجُّبًا الْمَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabati al-khalāʾiqu al-ḥāḍirīna min adabī wa-kāna aktharuhum taʿajjuban al-malika
sentences.l: and the creatures present marveled at my good manners, and the most amazed of them, in astonishment, was the king,
sentences.i: and everyone present marveled at my good manners — and none more amazed than the king himself,
sentences.n: الْحَاضِرِينَ keeps an accusative-looking ending though it describes the nominative subject الْخَلَائِقُ — another instance of this text's loose case-agreement.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ الْخَلْقَ بِالِانْصِرَافِ فَانْصَرَفُوا وَلَمْ يَبْقَ إِلَّا أَنَا وَحَضْرَةُ الْمَلِكِ وَالطَّوَاشِي وَمَمْلُوكٌ صَغِيرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma amara al-maliku al-khalqa bi-al-inṣirāfi fa-inṣarafū wa-lam yabqa illā anā wa-ḥaḍratu al-maliki wa-al-ṭawāshī wa-mamlūkun ṣaghīrun
sentences.l: Then the king ordered the people to withdraw, so they withdrew, and none remained except me, and the king's presence, and the eunuch, and a young page,
sentences.i: Then the king ordered everyone to withdraw, and they left, until none remained but me, the king himself, the eunuch, and a young page,
sentences.n: حَضْرَةُ الْمَلِكِ, literally 'the king's presence,' is an honorific way of naming the king himself. الطَّوَاشِي, 'eunuch,' is a loanword common in this period's usage.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ فَقَلَّمُوا سُفْرَةَ الطَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma amara al-maliku fa-qallamū sufrata al-ṭaʿāmi
sentences.l: Then the king gave an order, and they trimmed the food-tray,
sentences.i: Then the king gave an order, and the food-tray was brought in,
sentences.n: قَلَّمُوا (form II of قَلَّمَ, properly 'to trim, pare' — nails, a pen) does not fit a food-tray being set out; it is very likely a slip, in the edition or its transcription, for قَدَّمُوا, 'they brought forth, served' (a دّ/لّ confusion), the sense followed in the translation. The rasm is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَفِيهَا مَا هَشَّ وَطَارَ وَتَنَاكَحَ فِي الْأَوْكَارِ مِنَ الْقَطَا وَالسُّمَانِي وَسَائِرِ أَصْنَافِ الطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-fīhā mā hashsha wa-ṭāra wa-tanākaḥa fī al-awkāri mina al-qaṭā wa-al-sumānā wa-sāʾiri aṣnāfi al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: and in it was whatever had rustled and flown and mated in the nests, of sand-grouse, and quail, and the rest of the kinds of birds —
sentences.i: laden with every bird that had ever fluttered, flown, and paired in its nest — sand-grouse, quail, and every other kind of fowl —
sentences.n: مَا هَشَّ وَطَارَ وَتَنَاكَحَ فِي الْأَوْكَارِ is a stock merism for game birds in general, 'whatever flew and mated in nests', continued by the named species that follow. السُّمَانِي spells 'quail' (سُمَانَى) with a plain يَاء in place of the usual الف مقصورة — the two are interchangeable in this edition's typesetting; the final يَاء is left unmarked here, standing for the same -ā.

sentences.t: فَأَشَارَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى أَنَّ الْكُلَّ مَعَهُ فَقَعَدْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-ashāra al-maliku ilā anna al-kulla maʿahu fa-qaʿadtu
sentences.l: and the king gestured that all of it be with him, so I sat down —
sentences.i: and the king motioned for it all to be set before him and me together, so I sat down —
sentences.n: أَشَارَ إِلَى أَنَّ, 'gestured/signaled that' — the king keeps up his silence, established just above (only the eunuch and the page left with him), even in giving this instruction, by gesture rather than speech.

sentences.t:
لِلَّـه دَرُّ الشِّوا مَا كَانَ اَطْيَـبَه * وَالدُّهْنُ يُغْمَسُ فِي خَلِّ الْمَكَارِيجِ
مَا هَزَّنِي الْجُوعُ اِلَّا بِتُّ مُعْتَكِفًا * عَلَى الْهَرِيسَةِ فِي ضَوْءِ اللَّمَالِيجِ
sentences.tr:
lillāhi darru al-shiwā mā kāna aṭyabahu * wa-al-duhnu yughmasu fī khalli al-makārīji
mā hazzanī al-jūʿu illā bittu muʿtakifan * ʿalā al-harīsati fī ḍawʾi al-lamālīji
sentences.l:
God's is the excellence of the roast — how good it was! * — and its fat is dipped in the vinegar of the makārīj.
Hunger stirred me to nothing but this: I spent the night devoted * to the harīsa, in the light of the lamālīj.
sentences.i:
By God, how fine was the roast, how good it was! * — its fat dipped deep in the tangy vinegar sauce.
Hunger moved me to nothing else but to keep vigil * over the harīsa, by the gleam of the lamps.
sentences.n: لِلَّـه دَرُّ…, literally 'God's is the excellence of…,' is a fixed idiom of praise; مَا كَانَ أَطْيَبَهُ repeats the exclamation in the tafḍīl pattern, 'how tasty it was!' الْمَكَارِيجِ and اللَّمَالِيجِ are both obscure terms for utensils or vessels, not securely attested in Lane or Hava; rendered by context (a dipping-dish; a lamp, or perhaps 'spoon', from root ل-م-ج 'to taste a little'). بِتُّ مُعْتَكِفًا, literally 'I spent the night in devotion/seclusion' (اعتكاف elsewhere names religious retreat), is used hyperbolically of devotion to food. Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be; only the joins (' * ' and the line break) are ours.

sentences.t:
نَبَّهْتُهُ عِنْدَ أَكْلٍ فِي فُكَاهَتِهِ * عَلَى الْمَوَابِلِ أَصْنَافُ الدِّيَابِيجِ
يَا نَفْسُ صَبْرًا فَإِنَّ الدَّهْرَ ذُو عَجَبٍ * إِنْ ضَاقَ يَوْمًا أَتَانَا بِالتَّفَارِيجِ
sentences.tr:
nabbahtuhu ʿinda aklin fī fukāhatihi * ʿalā al-mawābili aṣnāfu al-diyābīji
yā nafsu ṣabran fa-inna al-dahra dhū ʿajabin * in ḍāqa yawman atānā bi-al-tafārīji
sentences.l:
I roused him, at a meal, in his merriment, * unto the trays — kinds of brocade.
O soul, [be] patient! For time holds wonder: * if it grows strait one day, it brings us relief.
sentences.i:
I called him to the feast, amid his mirth, * to trays spread with every kind of brocade.
O soul, be patient — for time is full of wonders: * let it grow strait one day, and it brings us relief.
sentences.n: Both these lines are printed with no tashkīl at all in the archive and are vocalised here as prose would be — unlike the couplet just before them, which the edition already points. الْمَوَابِلِ, 'trays' (?), is not securely attested and is rendered by context; the antecedent of the pronouns in نَبَّهْتُهُ / فُكَاهَتِهِ is left unclear in the Arabic — possibly the king, drawn to share the feast. التَّفَارِيج, 'openings, reliefs' (root ف-ر-ج), echoes the proverb al-faraj baʿda al-shidda, 'relief after hardship.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُمْتُ وَجَلَسْتُ بَعِيدًا
sentences.tr: thumma qumtu wa-jalastu baʿīdan
sentences.l: Then I rose and sat far off,
sentences.i: Then I got up and withdrew a little way off,

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى مَا كَتَبْتُهُ وَقَرَأَهُ فَتَعَجَّبَ
sentences.tr: fa-naẕara al-maliku ilā mā katabtuhu wa-qaraʾahu fa-taʿajjaba
sentences.l: and the king looked at what I had written, and read it, and marveled,
sentences.i: and the king examined what I had written, read it through, and marveled,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا لَلْعَجَبِ قِرْدٌ وَيَكُونُ عِنْدَهُ هَذِهِ الْفَصَاحَةُ وَالْخَطُّ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā li-al-ʿajabi qirdun wa-yakūnu ʿindahu hādhihi al-faṣāḥatu wa-al-khaṭṭu
sentences.l: and said: 'O the wonder of it — an ape, and there is with him this eloquence and this hand!
sentences.i: and said: 'What a wonder — an ape possessed of such eloquence and such a hand!
sentences.n: يَا لَلْعَجَبِ, literally 'O for the wonder,' is a fixed exclamation of astonishment, with لِـ marking the object of the exclamatory summons (the pattern يَا لِـ, 'oh, what a…!').

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ هَذَا مِنْ أَعْجَبِ الْعَجَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi inna hādhā min aʿjabi al-ʿajabi
sentences.l: By God, indeed this is among the most wondrous of wonders.'
sentences.i: By God, this is the strangest wonder of all.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُدِّمَ لِلْمَلِكِ مَشْرُوبٌ خَاصٌّ فِي زُجَاجٍ
sentences.tr: thumma quddima li-al-maliki mashrūbun khāṣṣun fī zujājin
sentences.l: Then a special drink was brought to the king, in glass,
sentences.i: Then a special drink was brought in for the king, in glass vessels,

sentences.t: فَشَرِبَ الْمَلِكُ ثُمَّ نَاوَلَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-shariba al-maliku thumma nāwalanī
sentences.l: and the king drank, then he handed [it] to me,
sentences.i: and the king drank, then passed it to me,

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلْتُ الْأَرْضَ وَشَرِبْتُ وَكَتَبْتُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbaltu al-arḍa wa-sharibtu wa-katabtu ʿalayhi
sentences.l: and I kissed the ground, and I drank, and I wrote upon it:
sentences.i: and I kissed the ground, drank, and wrote upon the cup:

sentences.t:
اَحْرَقُوني بِالنَّارِ يَسْتَنْطِقُوني * وَجَدُوني عَلَى الْبَلَاءِ صَبُورا
لِاَجْلِ هَذَا حَمَلْتُ فَوْقَ الْاَيَادِي * وَاَثِمْتُ مِنَ الْمِلَاحِ الثُّغُورَا
sentences.tr:
aḥraqūnī bi-al-nāri yastanṭiqūnī * wajadūnī ʿalā al-balāʾi ṣabūran
li-ajli hādhā ḥamaltu fawqa al-ayādī * wa-athimtu mina al-milāḥi al-thughūrā
sentences.l:
They burned me with fire, making me speak; * they found me, under trial, patient.
For this I bore [myself] above the hands; * and I made the mouths of the fair ones sin.
sentences.i:
They burned me in fire to make me confess — * and found me steadfast under the trial.
For this I am borne aloft on men's hands, * and through me the lips of the fair have sinned.
sentences.n: Spoken in wine's own voice, a common conceit of khamriyya (wine poetry): the grape is 'burned' — pressed and fermented — as if put to torture to yield its secret, and found patient under it. حَمَلْتُ is printed as an active perfect, 'I carried, I bore', though the sense wants a passive, 'I was borne [up in men's hands]', as the cup is raised in a toast; the archive's own vocalization is kept and the mismatch flagged rather than silently repaired. أَثِمْتُ (form I, ordinarily intransitive, 'I sinned') is likewise printed governing الثُّغُورَا directly as if a direct object, 'made-sin the mouths' — again kept exactly as pointed. Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be; only the joins are ours.

sentences.t:
هَتَفَ الصُّبْحُ بِالدُّجَى فَاسْقِنِيهَا * خَمْرَةً تَتْرُكُ الْحَلِيمَ سَفِيها
لَسْتُ اَدْرِي لِرِقَّةٍ وَصَفَاءٍ * هِيَ فِي كَاسِهَا اَمِ الْكَاسُ فِيهَا
sentences.tr:
hatafa al-ṣubḥu bi-al-dujā fa-isqinīhā * khamratan tatruku al-ḥalīma safīhan
lastu adrī li-riqqatin wa-ṣafāʾin * hiya fī kāsihā ami al-kāsu fīhā
sentences.l:
The dawn called out to the darkness — so give me to drink of her, * a wine that leaves the forbearing man a fool.
I do not know, for delicacy and clarity, * whether she is in her cup, or the cup is in her.
sentences.i:
Dawn has cried out against the dark — so pour me * a wine that turns the wise man into a fool.
So fine, so clear, I cannot tell * if she is in her cup, or the cup in her.
sentences.n: A classic khamriyya conceit closes the poem — wine so fine and its glass so pure the two blur into one another. فِي in the second line's 'هِيَ فِي كَاسِهَا' is the one word in this whole quatrain printed with no mark at all and is vocalised here; every other word of these four lines is copied exactly as pointed in the archive.

sentences.t: قَٰلَ فَقَرَأَ الْمَلِكُ الشِّعْرَ فَتَحَسَّرَ وَقَالَ لَوْكَانَ هَذَا الْأَدَبُ فِي إِنْسَانٍ لَفَاقَ أَهْلَ عَصْرِهِ وَزَمَانِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-qaraʾa al-maliku al-shiʿra fa-taḥassara wa-qāla law kāna hādhā al-adabu fī insānin la-fāqa ahla ʿaṣrihi wa-zamānihi
sentences.l: He said: Then the king read the poem and sighed [in wonder], and said, 'If this refinement were in a human, he would surpass the people of his age and his time.'
sentences.i: He relates: The king read the poem and could not help sighing in admiration, and said, 'If a human being possessed this much refinement, he would surpass everyone of his generation.'
sentences.n: قَالَ here is spelled defectively قل in the archive, missing its long ا — the same defective spelling recurs below (P97L18); it seems to work as the narrator's own resumption-tag, since this whole tale is told in the first person by the young man who was the ape, so 'he said' momentarily steps outside his own voice to mark that the account continues. تَحَسَّرَ carries its sense of an admiring sigh of longing ('if only…'), not grief.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَدَّمَ الْمَلِكُ رُقْعَةَ شِطْرَنْجٍ وَقَالَ هَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَلْعَبَ مَعِي
sentences.tr: thumma qaddama al-maliku ruqʿata shiṭranjin wa-qāla hal laka an talʿaba maʿī
sentences.l: Then the king brought forward a chessboard, and said, 'Have you [a mind] to play with me?'
sentences.i: Then the king brought out a chessboard and said, 'Would you like to play with me?'
sentences.n: هَلْ لَكَ أَنْ + subjunctive is an idiomatic invitation, literally 'is there for you [an inclination] that you should…' — rendered here as 'would you like to…?'

sentences.t: فَأَشَرْتُ بِرَاسِي نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ashartu bi-rāsī naʿam
sentences.l: So I gestured with my head: 'Yes.'
sentences.i: So I nodded my head: yes.
sentences.n: The narrator here is the young man who, at this point in the story, is still trapped in the shape of an ape and so cannot speak; he answers by nodding, as again below. بِرَاسِي is this text's colloquial spelling of Classical بِرَأْسِي, 'with my head' — the hamza simply not written, as with رَاسَكَ and رَاسَ elsewhere in this style of prose.

sentences.t: تَقَلَّمْتُ وَوَضَعْتُ الشِّطْرَنْجَ وَ لَعِبْتُ مَعَهُ مَرَّتَيْنِ وَأَنَا أَغْلِبُهُ فَحَارَ عَقْلُ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: taqallamtu wa-waḍaʿtu al-shiṭranja wa laʿibtu maʿahu marratayni wa-anā aghlibuhu fa-ḥāra ʿaqlu al-maliki
sentences.l: I [stepped up(?)], and I set out the chess[board], and I played with him twice, while I defeated him, so the king's mind reeled.
sentences.i: I stepped up, set out the board, and played against him twice, beating him both times, so that the king's mind reeled in astonishment.
sentences.n: تَقَلَّمْتُ keeps the archive's own letters ت-ق-ل-م-ت, pointed here as a form-V verb by default; the sense plainly wants something like 'I came/stepped forward' — what Classical تَقَدَّمْتُ would give — so this may be a compositor's slip of ل for د, or an otherwise unattested form; the letters are kept exactly as printed rather than silently corrected. The lone وَ before لَعِبْتُ is the archive's own line-break artifact: the connective for 'and I played' fell at the edge of the printed line and is set as its own token, the next word beginning bare on the following line; this recurs three more times below (before نَظَرَ, before أَنَا, and before قَالَ at the head of the next sentence) and is kept exactly as printed each time, exactly as the parallel night's own note on this same phenomenon does, rather than silently rejoined into واو العطف + the next word.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَأَخَذْتُ الدَّوَاةَ وَالْقَلَمَ وَكَتَبْتُ عَلَى الرُّقْعَةِ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma wa-akhadhtu al-dawāta wa-al-qalama wa-katabtu ʿalā al-ruqʿati hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then, and I took the inkstand and the pen, and I wrote on the board these two verses:
sentences.i: Then I took up the inkstand and pen, and wrote on the board these two verses:
sentences.n: ثُمَّ وَ, 'then, and,' stacks the two connectives, as this narrative style often does.

sentences.t:
جَيْشَانِ يَقْتَتِلَانِ طُولَ نَهَارِهِمْ * وَقِتَالُهُمْ فِي كُلِّ وَقْتٍ زَايِدْ
حَتَّى إِذَا جَنَّ الظَّلَامُ عَلَيْهِمْ * نَامَا جَمِيعًا فِي فِرَاشٍ وَاحِدْ
sentences.tr:
jayshāni yaqtatilāni ṭūla nahārihim * wa-qitāluhum fī kulli waqtin zāyid
ḥattā idhā janna al-ẕalāmu ʿalayhim * nāmā jamīʿan fī firāshin wāḥid
sentences.l:
Two armies fighting each other the length of their day, * and their fighting increasing at every moment;
until, when darkness fell upon them, * the two of them slept together in one bed.
sentences.i:
Two armies contend with one another the whole day long, * their battle growing ever fiercer with the hour;
but when darkness closes over them, * together the two lie down to sleep in a single bed.
sentences.n: The chess conceit: the black and white pieces are two 'armies' (جَيْش can mean either) that battle all day and, once put away at nightfall, rest together in the one board or box. Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be, including its end-rhyme forms without tanwīn (زَايِدْ, وَاحِدْ).

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا قَرَأَ الْمَلِكُ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ عَجِبَ وَطَرِبَ وَلَحِقَهُ الِانْبِهَارُ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā qaraʾa al-maliku hādhayni al-baytayni ʿajiba wa-ṭariba wa-laḥiqahu al-inbihāru
sentences.l: He said: And when the king had read these two verses, he marveled and was delighted, and astonishment overtook him,
sentences.i: He relates: When the king read these two verses, he marveled and was delighted, and astonishment overcame him,
sentences.n: الِانْبِهَار, 'astonishment,' is a form-VII verbal noun (اِنْفِعَال pattern) whose initial hamza is hamzat al-waṣl, never marked with our supplied hamza sign.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَ لِخَادِمِهِ اِمْضِ إِلَى سِتِّكَ سِتِّالْحُسْنِ وَقُلْ لَهَا كَلِّمِي الْمَلِكَ حَتَّى تَجِيءَ تَتَفَرَّجُ عَلَى هَذَا الْقِرْدِ الْعَجِيبِ
sentences.tr: wa qāla li-khādimihi imḍi ilā sittika sitti al-ḥusni wa-qul lahā kallimī al-malika ḥattā tajīʾa tatafarraja ʿalā hādhā al-qirdi al-ʿajībi
sentences.l: and he said to his servant: 'Go to your lady, Sitt al-Husn, and say to her: Speak with the king, so that she may come and look upon this wondrous ape.'
sentences.i: and he said to his chamberlain, 'Go to your lady, Sitt al-Husn, and tell her the king wishes to speak with her — so that she may come and see this wondrous ape.'
sentences.n: كَلِّمِي الْمَلِكَ, 'speak with the king' (form-II imperative, 2fs, quoted as the words the servant is to relay), works here as a summons formula — a pretext to bring the princess to see the ape, not a literal request that she open a conversation. سِتّ الْحُسْن, 'Sitt al-Husn' — literally 'the Lady of Beauty' — is the princess's own name and title throughout the tale.

sentences.t: فَغَابَ الطَّوَاشِي وَعَادَ وَمَعَهُ السِّتُّ
sentences.tr: fa-ghāba al-ṭawāshī wa-ʿāda wa-maʿahu al-sittu
sentences.l: So the eunuch went off, and he returned, and with him the Lady.
sentences.i: So the eunuch went off, and came back, bringing the Lady with him.
sentences.n: الطَّوَاشِي, 'the eunuch,' is the same servant just called خَادِم, and, in the princess's own words below, will be called الْمُقَدَّم, 'the chamberlain' — the eunuch who raised her. السِّتُّ, 'the Lady,' is short for سِتّ الْحُسْن.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَتْ إِلَيَّ غَطَّتْ وَجْهَهَا وَقَالَتْ يَا أَبِي كَيْفَ طَابَ عَلَى قَلْبِكَ أَنْ تُرْسِلَ خَلْفِي تُفَرِّجُنِي عَلَى الرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẕarat ilayya ghaṭṭat wajhahā wa-qālat yā abī kayfa ṭāba ʿalā qalbika an tursila khalfī tufarrijunī ʿalā al-rijāli
sentences.l: And when she looked at me, she covered her face, and said, 'O my father, how did it please your heart that you should send after me, to show me to the men?'
sentences.i: When she caught sight of me, she covered her face and said, 'Father, how could you bring yourself to send for me, to make me look at strange men?'
sentences.n: طَابَ عَلَى قَلْبِكَ, literally 'it grew sweet upon your heart,' is an idiom for something settling easily with someone — 'how could you bring yourself to…?' تُفَرِّجُنِي عَلَى (form-II فَرَّجَ, causative of 'to look, be diverted,' + عَلَى) is 'to show, display X to,' here 'make me look at.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا سِتَّالْحُسْنِ مَا عِنْدِي سِوَى الْمَمْلُوكِ الصَّغِيرِ وَالْمُقَدَّمِ الَّذِي رَبَّاكِي وَأَنَا أَبُوكِي فَمِنْ مَنْ تُغَطِّي وَجْهَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā sitta al-ḥusni mā ʿindī siwā al-mamlūki al-ṣaghīri wa-al-muqaddami alladhī rabbāki wa-anā abūki fa-min man tughaṭṭī wajhaki
sentences.l: So he said, 'O Sitt al-Husn, I have none but the little page, and the chamberlain who raised you, and I, your father — so from whom do you cover your face?'
sentences.i: He said, 'O Sitt al-Husn, there is no one here but the young page and the eunuch who raised you, and myself, your father — so from whom are you veiling your face?'
sentences.n: رَبَّاكِي and أَبُوكِي keep the extra ي the edition prints after the 2fs form (رَبَّاكِ, أَبُوكِ would be the plain Classical spellings) — the same colloquial-leaning habit as عَرَفْتِي below. فَمِنْ مَنْ, 'so from whom,' is this text's way of writing what a fuller Classical spelling would give as فَمِمَّنْ; kept as the two separate words the archive prints.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ إِنَّ هَذَا الْقِرْدَ شَابٌّ اِبْنُ مَلِكٍ وَأَبُوهُ اِسْمُهُ أَنْتِيمَارُوسُ صَاحِبُ جَزَائِرِ أَبَنُوسٍ وَهُوَ مَسْحُورٌ سَحَرَهُ الْعِفْرِيتُ جِرْجِيسُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat inna hādhā al-qirda shābbun ibnu malikin wa-abūhu ismuhu Antīmārūsu ṣāḥibu jazāʾiri abanūsin wa-huwa masḥūrun saḥarahu al-ʿifrītu Jirjīsu
sentences.l: So she said: 'Indeed, this ape is a young man, son of a king, and his father — his name is Antimarus, lord of the Isles of Ebony; and he is enchanted — the efrit Jirjis enchanted him,
sentences.i: She said, 'This ape is in truth a young man, the son of a king — his father's name is Antimarus, lord of the Ebony Isles — and he has been placed under a spell; the jinni Jirjis enchanted him,
sentences.n: أَنْتِيمَارُوس (Antimarus) is the prince's father, king of جَزَائِر أَبَنُوس, the 'Isles of Ebony'; the archive gives this as a plain construct, أَبَنُوس with no article. جِرْجِيس (Jirjis) is the efrit/jinni responsible for the spell — his own lineage is given in the next sentence.

sentences.t: الَّذِي هُوَ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ إِبْلِيسَ وَقَتَلَ زَوْجَتَهُ بِنْتَ مَلِكِ أَفْتَامُوسَ
sentences.tr: alladhī huwa min dhurriyyati Iblīsa wa-qatala zawjatahu binta maliki Aftāmūsa
sentences.l: who is of the progeny of Iblis, and he killed his [the prince's] wife, the daughter of King Aftamus,
sentences.i: who is descended from Iblis himself, and who murdered the prince's wife, the daughter of King Aftamus,
sentences.n: إِبْلِيس, Iblīs, is Satan/the Devil of Islamic tradition. زَوْجَتَهُ, 'his wife,' refers back to the enchanted prince, not to Jirjīs — it is Jirjīs who commits the murder described here. أَفْتَامُوس (Aftamus) is the murdered princess's father, otherwise unmentioned in this slice.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا الَّذِي تَزْعُمُ أَنَّهُ قِرْدٌ هُوَ رَجُلٌ عَالِمٌ عَاقِلٌ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā alladhī tazʿumu annahu qirdun huwa rajulun ʿālimun ʿāqilun
sentences.l: And this one whom you suppose to be an ape is [in truth] a learned, wise man.
sentences.i: And this one you take for an ape is in truth a learned and intelligent man.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْمَلِكُ مِنِ ابْنَتِهِ وَ نَظَرَ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ أَحَقٌّ مَا تَقُولُ عَنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-maliku mini ibnatihi wa naẕara ilayya wa-qāla aḥaqqun mā taqūlu ʿanka
sentences.l: So the king marveled at his daughter, and looked at me, and said: 'Is what she says about you true?'
sentences.i: The king marveled at his daughter, and turned to look at me, and said, 'Is what she says about you true?'

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ بِرَاسِي نَعَمْ وَبَكَيْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu bi-rāsī naʿam wa-bakaytu
sentences.l: So I said with my head: 'Yes,' and I wept.
sentences.i: So I nodded my head, yes, and wept.
