sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْمَلِكُ مِنْ أَيْنَ عَرَفْتِي أَنَّهُ مَسْحُورٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-maliku min ayna ʿaraftī annahu masḥūrun
sentences.l: So the king said to her: 'From where did you know that he is enchanted?'
sentences.i: The king said to her, 'How did you know that he was under a spell?'
sentences.n: عَرَفْتِي keeps the extra ي the edition prints after the 2fs perfect ending — a colloquial-leaning spelling for Classical عَرَفْتِ.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَا أَبَتِ كَانَ عِنْدِي وَ أَنَا صَغِيرَةٌ عَجُوزٌ مَاكِرَةٌ سَاحِرَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā abati kāna ʿindī wa anā ṣaghīratun ʿajūzun mākiratun sāḥiratun
sentences.l: So she said: 'O my father, there was with me, while I was young, an old woman, cunning, a sorceress,
sentences.i: She said, 'O my father, when I was a little girl, there was an old woman with me — a cunning sorceress —
sentences.n: يَا أَبَتِ, 'O my father,' is a fixed vocative with the archaic تِ ending standing in for a possessive 'my.'

sentences.t: فَعَلَّمَتْنِي السِّحْرَ وَصِنَاعَتَهُ وَقَٰلَ حَفِظْتُهُ وَأَتْقَنْتُهُ وَحَفِظْتُ مِنْهُ مِائَةً وَسَبْعِينَ بَابًا مِنْ أَبْوَابِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿallamatnī al-siḥra wa-ṣināʿatahu wa-qāla ḥafiẕtuhu wa-atqantuhu wa-ḥafiẕtu minhu miʾatan wa-sabʿīna bāban min abwābihi
sentences.l: So she taught me sorcery and its craft — and (he says): 'I had memorized it and mastered it' — and I had memorized from it a hundred and seventy chapters of its chapters,
sentences.i: She taught me sorcery and its craft, and I memorized it and mastered it thoroughly, learning by heart a hundred and seventy of its chapters,
sentences.n: قَالَ here is again spelled defectively قل (see the note on the first sentence of this slice); embedded inside the princess's own first-person account, it oddly reasserts 'he said' where no third person is speaking — most likely the same recurring narrator's tag, the prince (telling his whole story in the first person) marking that he is still relating what follows, even inside his own quotation of her words. Kept in the literal layer; smoothed away in the idiomatic one, since English has no equivalent tic. مِائَةً keeps the edition's own precomposed hamza letter (ئ), exactly as printed, per the rule for words the edition itself already points with a hamza sign.

sentences.t: أَقَلُّ بَابٍ فِيهِ أُخَلِّي حِجَارَةَ مَدِينَتِكَ خَلْفَ جَبَلِ قَافٍ وَأَجْعَلُهَا لُجَّةَ بَحْرٍ وَأَجْعَلُ أَهْلَهَا سَمَكًا فِي وَسَطِهَا
sentences.tr: aqallu bābin fīhi ukhallī ḥijārata madīnatika khalfa jabali qāfin wa-ajʿaluhā lujjata baḥrin wa-ajʿalu ahlahā samakan fī wasaṭihā
sentences.l: The least chapter of it — I could move the stones of your city beyond Mount Qaf, and make it the depths of a sea, and make its people fish within it.
sentences.i: The least of its chapters would let me carry the very stones of your city beyond Mount Qaf, turn it into the depths of a sea, and turn its people into fish swimming within it.
sentences.n: جَبَل قَاف, Mount Qaf, is the legendary mountain range Islamic cosmology imagines ringing the edge of the world — a byword for an unimaginably remote place.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُوهَا يَا بِنْتِي بِحَيَاتِي خَلِّصِي لَنَا هَذَا الشَّابَّ حَتَّى أَجْعَلَهُ وَزِيرِي لِأَنَّهُ شَابٌّ ظَرِيفٌ لَبِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla abūhā yā bintī bi-ḥayātī khalliṣī lanā hādhā al-shābba ḥattā ajʿalahu wazīrī li-annahu shābbun ẕarīfun labībun
sentences.l: So her father said: 'O my daughter, by my life, free for us this young man, so that I may make him my vizier, for he is a young man, refined, intelligent.'
sentences.i: Her father said, 'My daughter, for my life's sake, free this young man for us, that I may make him my vizier — for he is a clever and refined young man.'
sentences.n: بِحَيَاتِي, 'by my life,' is an entreaty formula. خَلِّصِي (form-II imperative, 2fs, 'free, deliver, disenchant') takes هَذَا الشَّابَّ directly as its object.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: So she said to him: 'With love and honor.'
sentences.i: She answered him, 'Gladly, and with honor.'
sentences.n: حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً is a fixed idiom of ready, willing consent — still used today — literally 'with love and with honor.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَتْ يَدَهَا سِكِّينًا وَعَمِلَتْ دَائِرَةً
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhat yadahā sikkīnan wa-ʿamilat dāʾiratan
sentences.l: Then she took, [in] her hand, a knife, and made a circle.
sentences.i: Then she took a knife in hand and drew a circle.
sentences.n: يَدَهَا stands in the accusative without the preposition بِ that Classical usage would supply (بِيَدِهَا, 'with her hand') — another instance of this text's habit of dropping a preposition after a verb of taking or seizing. This is where the archived text itself breaks off: the princess has just begun her own counter-working against Jirjīs, drawing the circle for it, when dawn cuts the telling short.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥ
sentences.l: And the dawn overtook Shahrazad, so she fell silent from the licit speech.
sentences.i: And dawn overtook Shahrazad, and she fell silent, breaking off from the tale she was permitted to tell.
sentences.n: The fixed formula that closes every night of the frame story: Shahrazad's telling is only 'licit' (مُبَاح) up until daybreak, by her arrangement with the king, so dawn cuts her off here mid-story.
